This review is a direct reply to all the negative reviews saying that the combat is clunky.

First: I am a total metroidvania noob. I just found interest in the genre a few days ago and this is the first game I am playing. I'm not experienced and also not a die-hard fan who plays every title that comes out.

From those reviews, I get the impression that the authors went into the game expecting a hack'n'slay action game. And that is why they were disappointed. "Lost Ruins" is not about rapidly hitting your buttons and slashing though enemies.

There ARE enemies that are easiest to defeat if you rush in and hit them before they know what is happening. More often than not though, you need to know what you are doing. Think of it as a beat'em'up, as if you were playing "Guilty Gear". If you mess up, the enemy can often get you in a stunlock and kill you no matter how many HP you had, especially if you face several enemies at once. At the very least, you will lose a lot of HP. If you know how you have to approach an enemy, chances are you can down him without losing any HP at all.

Such was the case with the first boss, which frustrated me massively. It didn't help that I was playing the demo and that you couldn't skip cutscenes there (you can in the proper game). Once I found out how to kill the minions and then the boss, I am confident I can do so without getting hit at all. It's not even about hit zones or immunities, it's just movement and attack patterns.

The game doesn't want to give you endless action. It's about ressource management and tactical combat movements. The gratification does not come from going in with guns blazing and slaying foe after foe, but from executing just the right movements in just the right timing. That's not to say the game has no speedrun potential, in the contrary. I'm sure you can rush through it if you perfectly memorized each enemy's patterns.

Now the game HAS its downsides. Consumables, especially ranged attacks, are semi-finite. You get money and the occasional item from drops and opponents respawn, but mana does not regenerate (HP can, to an extent) and potions are really expensive. This makes me not use anything at all except for boss fights. There are also no quick-use slots for consumables so you have to enter the menu each time, and with a lot of very situational consumables you often don't end up using them even when it would be beneficial. Which is not a real problem if you can stand retrying a room over and over and are not playing hardcore mode or speedrunning.

The characters are interesting and quirky and there is a slightly clichéd but entertaining story unfolding. I'm 3 hours in (2 more hours in the demo) and just facing the second boss, and I still like what I am seeing.

Having passed the point where I can refund this game, I can safely say this game is a gem.

Yes, there's a lot of cute girls. Hell, one of the bosses is a giant slime girl in an area partially inhabited by normal sized slime girls. But push all that aside for a second and just listen to me.

This game is a metroidvania that punishes you for trying to play it like most others. Your dodge ability is slow and clunky. You character is fragile and can die fairly quickly. Your weapons are either slow to swing or lacking in range. The game is stacked against you in every possible way; fighting foes face-to-face is INCREDIBLY dangerous. I've often said people overhype the difficulty of Dark Souls, but this game somehow manages to live up to the hype of a completely different series by being every bit as brutally punishing as FromSoft's work is hyped up to be.

However, this game is not unbeatable. It is a thinking man's metroidvania. Don't think through problems; think around them. The game gives you ample resources; I've actually found myself using things like consumable wands, thrown items and spells very frequently to avoid direct confrontation, and whenever I was forced into a face-to-face fight, I used proper spacing to maximize distance between me and my opponent so that once I landed a hit, I could escape before they could retaliate. You're a scared, confused schoolgirl, not a trained warrior. Once you understand how the game is meant to be played and pick up on the way it encourages you to approach situations, it becomes a blast.

Let me give an example. The second boss's arena has cages with goblins inside. These cages can and will be knocked down during your battle, but the goblins just stand there and cower. During phase 2, the boss will eat these goblins to heal itself; in my first couple of fights, I made the mistake of ignoring that and ran out of resources quickly and died. However, there is a finite number of these goblins. So I decided to just hit it once, back off, let it heal, then rinse and repeat; then, once it was out of healing resources, I used my consumable buffs and spells to steamroll the boss.

This is the beauty of Lost Ruins. It deserves every ounce of the praise it has received and then some. I can absolutely see myself running the game on a higher difficulty once I beat it.

And for those of you intimidated by the game, there is an Accessible difficulty; I'm not someone who believes hard games NEED easy modes per se, but if a developer wishes to implement one, it's always appreciated.

Try the game! And I hope you enjoy it as much as I am.

8/10 This game is pretty good. (9/10 for me personally)

The Story - itself is what i would say is the 'DMC3 effect' where in that it's entertaining as hell but has some surprising depth to it (and some dark messed up implications) that at some points gave me the feels.

Gameplay - will be quite difficult for new players as it was for me but once you narrow down the mechanics it feels really good with all the weapons, ranged weapons and magic at your disposal. The variety of builds you can conjure up is astounding. Not to mention the amazing enemy variety that the game presents that will keep things not only entertaining but challenging as well. Likewise, the bosses really test your skills (and knowledge of mechanics as well).

Visuals - are gorgeous and aesthetically pleasing.

Loses points - due to the certain items being a bit too strong in that magic builds in the (very) late game are a bit too strong (for me personally). Inventory item swapping and usage (which you'll be doing a lot) can be streamlined further to lessen the monotony of it a bit. Finally, there should've been a new game plus for the veteran difficulty which in my opinion could've added late game enemies to the earlier stages whilst keeping your inventory so you can use all that OP stuff as well as your skill throughout a new replay. Maybe throw in even harder new enemies because why not?

Conclusion,

Instead of wasting money on some in-game micro-transaction, buy other games and experience something new. Lost Ruins is one of those experiences, simple and entertaining with surprising depth to it. Has its flaws yes, but it is an overall satisfying product in the end.

This is by a landslide THE MOST CLUNKY platformer I've EVER played!

The combat system needs A LOT of work.
- Weapon swings are stupidly slow. I actually cringed when I first picked up the gladius and tried it out. If you give a real life mace to a 7 year old, he's gonna swing it faster than the MC of this game swings a freaking gladius (which is designed for quick stabs btw, note to the devs).
- For some bizarre reason, the devs decided that when somebody extends their arm forward whilst jumping forward, all of their momentum from the jump magically disappears and you drop down like a rock...

Other than that, the game throws A LOT of cheap shots at you. For example: you're being conditioned to believe that your shield can block anything, including axe swings from orcs 10 times your size, or even explosive projectiles. Then there's that one random boss that damages you if you try to block it (which is a one-shot on veteran)...

Then there's the bosses... The design is pretty cool and the fights are entertaining, but a lot of them are very cheap and unnecessarily long. The ice boss for example: you triggered it, see the blizzard, cool effects and everything, then you get ready to fight it, but oh wait, you get insta hit if you didn't instantly jump on a platform after you regained control.
There are a lot of examples of such cheap shots. They're cheap shots because you're usually only going to get screwed over by them once.

Then there's the hitboxes... oh boy... suffice to say, they need A LOT of work. Often times you will stab an enemy, with your weapon literally overlapping the enemy, but no wait, the game decided you didn't actually hit it and proceeds to hit you instead. Then there are hits that land half a meter away from you, that still bizarrely hit you.

There's also the fact that they decided that the autosave shrines can't be re-triggered, so if it's right before a boss, enjoy having to keep switching your equipment around after every death, because there's no way to save again at the autosave shrines...

This game is an absolute treat for the senses.

The sound design is especially top-notch here. Someone spent time carefully planning overlapping sounds to not interfere too much with each other. Footsteps are responsive and sell the weight of characters and the surfaces they walk on. Ambient soundscapes pair well with any underscoring provided - and when there is silence it is with purpose! Actions and indicators are satisfyingly present with crisp transients and environment processing that's subtle but present... I know more and more games are taking sound design seriously these days, but when it's done right it's a treat and this game does it [i]very[/i] right.

Also, the visual detail is sublime for anyone who appreciates pixel aesthetics. We've got dynamic dithering on the dynamic shadows and dithering on the fade-out of the overlaying bokeh light effects in some scenes. Light maps paired with carefully applied shaders give a nice, glowy, rim-lighting effect when appropriate that doesn't distract from the pixel aesthetic. Animation is also buttery smooth with filtering turned on (feels a bit less polished with lower filtering settings, to me). Really, it's just plain gorgeous and does almost everything right where design rules apply. Might seem funny, but I think the least interesting visual detail to this game was the illustrated character busts seen during dialogue - and they don't look terrible or anything, they are just very static compared to the polish found everywhere else.

Gameplay is pleasant. I'm still playing on the default difficulty and have only died a couple times. 2D platformers aren't usually my thing, but after I got accustomed to the jump height and distance I didn't feel like that was much of a struggle (yet). Platform edges are consistent and the fall speed (without any buffs) is just floaty and precise enough to be comfortable for most players to land where they want. It wasn't long before they started giving me equipment that impacted movement, so I suspect progression will unlock some variety to better suit player preferences.

In classic, metroidvania fashion, progression and discovery work together to feel rewarding to the player. You expand your arsenal of abilities and equipment to reach new areas of the map that continue narration.

It's a simple system, but resource management is critical. You have some room for error, but you can easily get killed quickly if you rush everything and avoid a methodical approach to most situations. So far, it all feels very well-balanced on normal difficulty.

Animation, while very smooth to look at, may actually have been where I struggled the most at first. The first weapon you receive does not have an instantaneous attack, so there is a miniscule-but-present build-up time you have to account for while charging an enemy and swinging your sword. This was the most jarring yet fundamental mechanic for me to adapt to, but the game seems aware of this learning curve as you're given some fodder enemies to practice on (that can kill you, but at minor expense to your progression only) and literally the first item I purchased from the vending machine reduced my attack delay slightly. The silver-lining to the slow sword-swing was I noticed a visual-distortion effect on the trail behind the sword itself mid-swing that adds weight to the motion and eventual impact, even as the most basic weapon available. I think mastering the timing and distancing for effective attack strategies might actually appeal a bit to people that enjoy 2D fighters as I see some minor overlap. At the very least, it's not a game for button-mashing.

Overall, I'm just gushing. Other reviewers probably have more critical takes on the experience that appeal to the more challenge-proned players. I'm not at all surprised by how well this game is rated on Steam right now; it's very competently made.

I respect Lost Ruins on the basis that I understand it. The designers behind this, you and I are not so different. We like the same thing- cute, sometimes a little fucked up, anime monster girls. That is what this game is- a tour of and/or an excuse to meet a healthy cast of anime monster girls. And for that, I can say that I enjoyed my time with Lost Ruins. I will likely take some amount of effort to keep an eye on the artists behind this to see what else they do, simply because I liked the monster girls so much.

But, unfortunately, that's where my enjoyment basically comes to an end. The actual video game that's built around this monster girl tour... wasn't that great, really. Normally I enjoy these kinds of anime 2D metroidvanias. However, I think the blend of "survival" elements, and what I would consider the removal of real "metroidvania" elements really just did not vibe with me.
Without going into too many details, I would say that all of the elements in this game felt watered down in some way. The combat? Simple, slow, and honestly pretty clunky. Magic? Uninteresting, save for maybe the magic only run that has additional modifiers to make magic actually useful before the 3rd boss. Equipment? Mostly useless, didn't even get the maid outfit until the last 30 minutes of the game. Exploration? Painfully simple. Enemies respawn, and you don't ever get any additions to your moveset. What you have when you spawn in is what you get, and while that fits in with the Survival elements, it made me wholly uninterested in exploring.

The bosses, while designed very well of course, ultimately were a drag. Either painfully frustrating or pathetically easy. I beat the final boss on my 3rd try using the same strats as every other boss- hit her with a big weapon before she kills you. I can't say much since there aren't any real standout elements that I think are bad, persay, but it equally did not have any standout elements that were good.

The story is also pretty much nonexistent. It came off to me that the text here was translated, because it all felt a bit flat. But, I don't hold that against the game as I'm not one to harp on stories anyway. As I said previously this was a tour of cute monster girls, and the plot just facilitated our continued progress along that tour.

The only thing I'll say that genuinely upset me was locking the "true" ending behind the highest difficulty, without any indication that that's the case. I don't mind jumping through a few hoops to get the best ending (The "Don't open any chests until the last zone" quest is stupid, but I digress), but I have ZERO intentions of playing through the entire game again, even harder than before (Having cleared on "Recommended" previously), just for some extra dialog at the end. 
The unique game modes after the initial completion are interesting, especially the "Boss mode" which I briefly took a look at, but it just being a beat for beat run through the entire game again but with various restrictions just feels more like padding than actually interesting.

I will give this game a thumbs up, as I would not want to negatively affect the review score for this game. I will, however, say that if you do not find the idea of touring cute monster girl sprites interesting enough for you, then this probably isn't the experience for you.

While Lost Ruins comes off as a tad fan servicey at times, I have to say that I enjoyed the game quite a lot even during the a bit over the top moments on some of the boss battles. The metroidvania exploration style in this is more castlevania than metroid. I found the exploration in the game to be satisfying with minimal backtracking unless you wanted to find rooms you didn't get into previously. True to form of the castlevania inspiration, there's a bunch of post ending content with different variations of gameplay and even a mode that lets you play as some of the bosses with different plot points & events occurring across the game after you have beaten it, making it feel completely different than your original run. 

I also very much enjoyed the pixelated art design and style of the in game characters. The actual character art does come across as being a bit lewd and that's cool if it's your thing, but it felt borderline for me at times. The level designs were great and didn't feel amateur at all. Only thing with design side of things I took issue with aside from the over-lewd was some of the music got noticeably repetitive. Very big into OST's and I enjoyed the tracks the composer worked on, just noticed some of the tracks looped more than others. A solid attempt for the first game in the series. 

The gameplay is very rigid and I did not like the loss of momentum on jumps and attack swings mid air, but after a few minutes of getting used to the controls, it played nicely and I enjoyed the tight platforming. The sheer amount of item choice & playstyles available to you gets a bit overwhelming for the length of the game. By the time you get into the swing of things, a new drop changes things up. Might be a design choice by devs and that's good as I was switching my weapons constantly as well as spells and equipment. The games also proper challenging and will make you change things up or "git gud" at times, after a few retries you learn the swing of things and can overcome pretty quickly. 

I would def put this up there with indie metroidvania titles like Momadora, Deedlit in Wonder Labyrinth & Blasphamous that are under appreciated and shining examples of what pixel art games should look like. Def worth your time if you're a metroidvania fan. I am excited to watch Altari's next game, be it in the series or not. Hopefully wont miss their next kickstarter as I would have backed the project had I been aware. 

TL;DR Lost Ruins is a great metroidvania style game and worth your time if you don't mind the anime girls aesthetic as it can get a bit over the top on the fan service at times. Would pay 20-30 for the amount of content. I hope to see more from the developers when they are ready to release another game.

Lost Ruins is an action-packed 2D platformer that skillfully blends challenging combat, exploration, and RPG elements into a cohesive and engaging experience. Developed by Altari Games, it draws clear inspiration from classics like Castlevania and Dark Souls, offering players a dark, atmospheric world filled with menacing enemies, intricate level design, and deep customization options. The game’s pixel art style is both nostalgic and polished, creating a moody, immersive environment that invites players to delve into its mysterious and dangerous ruins.

One of the standout features of Lost Ruins is its combat system, which emphasizes timing, precision, and strategy. Unlike many platformers that rely on simple button-mashing, this game encourages players to learn enemy patterns and carefully manage stamina and positioning. The combat feels weighty and satisfying, with a variety of weapons and skills that allow for diverse playstyles. Whether you prefer quick, agile attacks or heavy, deliberate strikes, the game caters to multiple approaches while maintaining a consistent level of challenge throughout.

Exploration in Lost Ruins is rewarding and thoughtfully designed. The interconnected maps encourage backtracking and keen observation, with hidden secrets and shortcuts scattered throughout the environment. This design fosters a sense of discovery and progression that mirrors the classic Metroidvania formula. Players are often required to solve environmental puzzles or acquire new abilities to access previously unreachable areas, adding depth and variety to the gameplay loop. The world itself feels alive with history and danger, supported by haunting soundscapes and evocative pixel art that set an eerie tone.

Customization and progression are well-implemented, giving players meaningful control over their character’s development. A variety of weapons, armor, and magical skills can be unlocked and upgraded, allowing for tailored builds that enhance different aspects of combat and survivability. This RPG element adds a layer of depth, encouraging experimentation and replayability. The upgrade system also ties into the game’s lore, further immersing players in the world and its secrets.

The difficulty level in Lost Ruins is notable—challenging but fair. The game strikes a balance where failure is a learning experience rather than a source of frustration. Enemies are punishing, but patterns are discernible with practice, and the game’s checkpoints are placed thoughtfully to minimize tedious repetition. Boss encounters, in particular, stand out as memorable tests of skill, combining intricate attack patterns with atmospheric presentation that heightens the stakes.

Visually, Lost Ruins impresses with its detailed pixel art and atmospheric environments. Each area feels distinct, from dank caverns to ominous ruins, all rendered with care and a consistent aesthetic that complements the dark fantasy setting. The animations are fluid, giving life to both the player character and enemies, while lighting effects enhance the mood and tension.

The soundtrack and sound design play a crucial role in immersing players within the game’s world. The music ranges from somber and haunting to intense and adrenaline-pumping during combat, perfectly complementing the gameplay and narrative beats. Ambient sounds add depth to the environments, reinforcing the feeling of isolation and danger.

While Lost Ruins excels in many areas, it does have some minor drawbacks. The learning curve can be steep for newcomers, and certain sections may feel a bit repetitive due to the platforming challenges combined with combat. Additionally, some players might find the pixel art style too retro or simplistic compared to more modern visuals, though this is largely a matter of personal taste.

In conclusion, Lost Ruins is a compelling and well-crafted action-platformer that will appeal to fans of challenging gameplay and atmospheric worlds. Its blend of precise combat, rewarding exploration, and RPG customization creates a rich experience that keeps players engaged and motivated to uncover every secret. While demanding, it offers a satisfying sense of accomplishment with every victory. For those seeking a tough but fair adventure steeped in dark fantasy and classic influences, Lost Ruins stands out as a worthy and memorable journey.

-HP/MP does not regenerate naturally, even at a save point
-Attacks are clunky, slow and have poor hitboxes

-Air attacks stop all forward momentum
-Checkpoints are single-use (until you hit another checkpoint)
-Status ailments everywhere

It's designed to be playable with all these "downsides" so enemies are clunky and slow themselves, healing items are plentiful, and hard saves are frequent. A fairly short, mildly challenging action-platformer, with a more tactical focus than running straight into every enemy mindlessly. 

You will be punished if you try to do this. 

I was lead to believe that this game was going to be unforgiving. My experience, even on the "Recommended" Difficulty was hardly that. I died, sure, but never enough times to want to pull my hair out or quit playing altogether. 

That said, I didn't find it as challenging or as difficult as some reviews led me to believe, but the game is not an easy one either. They warn you outright upon starting a new game that this is not meant to be a quick "run and gun" experience. 

The Heroine, swings melee weapons slowly. Timing is important. Traps are appropriately dangerous, but relatively rare. Figuring out when to dodge is likewise, very important. Nothing particularly new here. 

I found a wide variety of weapons available, mostly swords, axes, daggers, and hammers. I never encountered any spears, as far as I am aware of. 

Ranged options are mostly down to various throwing weapons (both traditional and, uniquely, some throwing bottles), a few bows, and casting spells. It took me some time to encounter a bow, so if that's your preferred playstyle, be wary of that. You may not acquire one till an hour or more in. 

I like the interactions between various mechanics. Casting a Lightning spell while soaking wet is, obviously, a bad idea, and a quick way to kill yourself. Finding means to solve these moment to moment problems is definitely a treat. 

However, I want to preface that previous statement with confirmation that you will be doing quite a bit of inventory management. If you're suffering bleed stacks, you can die quickly. So you will find yourself going into the inventory very often to resolve various issues. Casting a fire spell, while covered in Oil is likewise, a bad idea. 

Also, if you do find yourself changing your routine to fight against a boss. The Green "Angel" Checkpoints will only store whatever version of your equipment you had as you passed them. So you will have to reset your equipment should you be stuck at a boss. 

I didn't find it annoying as other people did, but I can see why it would get frustrating. So I will also mention that here. 

All in all, I found it a fun, and occationally challenging experience that lasted a handful of hours.

Lost Ruins is a very simple and overall decent action platformer (not a metroidvania) . It is quite generic, feels overall quite solid, and its sprite work is probably the most standout thing about it. The difficulty is not crazy, and the game is easy to cheese, if that's what you want. I played the game for around 6 hours and nearly 100% completed it. If you're looking for something to play, get this on the cheap and it'll kill 6 hours—you could do far worse. 

[h1] Story & Presentation[/h1]
There isn't a whole lot to say about the story. It's not especially deep; the main playthrough has almost zero characterisation almost on any character—they're all quite bland. The premise is you've been summoned from another world and must kill *the things* in order to regain your memories and cue the highly predictable plot twist at the end. There are books scattered about for extra plot too, they're short and much like the story as a whole, don't outstay their welcome. 

In the post-game, a new mode unlocks that lets you play the story through in a different way, with some different characters that have actual personality. I have not finished this, but so far it is slightly more engaging?

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]
The gameplay is quite solid, but overly simple to be truly satisfying or anything above "average." You have melee weapons and magic. You have weapons that stab, swing overhead, some that are slow, and some that are fast. Your magic options are spinny balls of ice, fire, electric, or a projectile of those elements. There are a couple more creative ones, like invisibility, absorbing corpses and the like for HP, but again, nothing that'll rock your socks off. 

A positive that the game has is that accessories, and some weapons, have unique effects which are quite impactful and can create many OP or cheese strategies. You won't find boring "+1" attack damage armour, for instance. It's usually +50% bleed, +30% extra damage against orcs, etc. While in some senses these are mundane, they're big increases you can exploit. Some are way more unique, such as getting +1 HP regeneration when wet, or +3 HP regeneration when bleeding, immunity to being frozen and etc. While these are just generic immunities and buffs, they're impactful and you can FEEL their impact on gameplay, which can't be said for every game these days. It makes your choice of accessories quite impactful, and there are a lot of synergies and builds you can go for. It's simple and a bit of fun.

Another thing I liked was the interaction between elements. The game has reactions between elements, such as water being hit with an ice spell will freeze it, doing damage to enemies in it (and yourself). Gasoline can catch fire and deal fire damage. The game even messes with you in places with this, putting jars of gasoline and candles you can accidentally destroy to light yourself on fire. It isn't a complex system, but, like everything else, it's simple and a bit of fun.

[h1] Exploration [/h1]
Lost Ruins has a metroidvania-looking map, but for the most part, it's a long linear corridor to the end. It has branching paths that will reward your exploration with unique accessories and weapons, as described above. There's a decent variety of biomes available as well. It keeps it from being too samey. There's a good mix of enemy types, although all of them are super simple and quite easy to kill overall. They look and feel very good to fight against.

[h1] Bosses & General Combat [/h1]
The bosses in this game have great sprite work and vibrant animations for the most part and feel very alive. Sadly, the complexity of the combat system and their attacks don't reach that same bar of quality, unfortunately. They'll have very few attacks, often 3-4 they'll cycle between, sometimes they'll also just de-aggro and stand in the arena doing nothing while you heal? It's unfortunate.

Overall, "it's simple and a bit of fun." sums the game up in a sentence. The quality of experience varies; it has some issues here and there, and it's a shame the boss designs don't have gameplay that matches their quality, but that doesn't make it bad or terrible, just mediocre and okay.

This game sits in a rather interesting cross roads of genres. In basic concept and overarching gameplay loop, it's a Metroidvania. You explore a series of rooms making up an interconnected world, defeat bosses and gain upgrades or adjustments to your kit along the way.
That's about as far as the comparison goes however.
The moment to moment gameplay is not like any other Metroidvania, it's combat and attacks are slow and seemingly clunky. The fastest attacks still leave you standing still for a good while, and while you have a dodge roll it's start up and recovery times mean it's not good for much beyond dodging an attack and disengaging, you'll almost always get hit if you attack to counter after rolling. The game is rather difficult initially as a result, though I did play on the Veteran difficulty for my first play through.

However, this kind of gameplay is intentional, and the game is for the most part built around it. It's much less focused on the action of the gameplay, rather it rewards care in exploring the world and taking to careful preparation. The game lacks real upgrades to it, bosses drop stat upgrades or equipment slots rather than new abilities, and throughout the game you'll be collecting an entire variety of spells, weapons and accessories that can drastically modify your loadout and how you can approach situations. Early on the slow nature of combat made me gravitate towards the fastest weapon I could find, but soon I found that using a large heavy weapon was much more successful thanks to the range it gave me and the ability to control the fight by making enemies have to close the distance with me instead, and often times I could kill enemies in one or two hits. The game wants you to be slow and careful, and use the right tool for the job, and you'll be much more successful adjusting what your kit is depending on what you're fighting.

The game does have a bit of a difficulty issue around this though. Being very stingy with money and offering no free heals, the early game is arguably the hardest part of the game as you lack the tools needed to properly strategize and play around the situations in front of you. The first boss was certainly the hardest for me, even with equipment that let me move quickly or heal in her arena, it'd certainly have been even worse if I hadn't explored before approaching her. However by the mid game, with the proper use of consumables and equip loads I was able to start killing bosses in only a handful of hits, with the final boss needing less than ten hits if you set yourself up to deal large amounts of damage. As well, magic started out as a valuable and scarce resource in the early game that slowly became my main method of clearing out mobs once I'd gained items to let me passive regenerate mana in the late game. While being able to fight only with spells was cool, magic is also incredibly strong and much of the game's moment to moment difficulty was diminished. On one hand I was rewarded for gathering and using all the tools I could, but I given the ability to simply roll over any non boss enemy purely with spells. 

Also, dev if you read these, please add some kind of loadout system, often times I had to menu through a cluttered inventory as I wanted to get the achievements for collecting items and it became rather annoying to swap everything out even with a favorite's system. As well, the ability to resave at checkpoint statues instead of having to leave to activate a different one is a much needed QoL change.

Over all, I'd recommend the game. It's not a hack and slash, and shouldn't be approached that way. The art style obviously has a bit of a lewd anime girl trend in a similar vein to Shantae, but I wouldn't say it detracts from the game much and the overall aesthetic and featured art is quite good. There's not much to write home about on the story, it's alright with a decent twist at the end and some of the characters can be amusing or quirky.

Alright, so I know the review says I recommend this game (and I do), but it certainly isn't perfect. It's well worth the $20 USD I spent on it, though.

The storyline is pretty simple, but there's enough mystery to keep you engaged. The heroine just sorta appears, with no memory of what happened. Within your first few steps, someone named Beatrice shows up, and before too long she tells the heroine that the seal on her memory will be lifted if she can defeat the followers of the Dark Lady. Desperate to recover her memory, she embarks on her quest. The basic premise is simple enough, but as you play you find journal entries written by various people that either give you lore for the overall plot or the specific areas that you're in. That, along with the few NPCs that you DO find and do quests for, you get a pretty good idea of what the state of the world is. It's actually quite interesting to see what's going on in the world, and figuring out who the various NPCs who wrote the journals are.

Now that the story is out of the way, let's talk about the actual mechanics of the game. Since the review is positive, I'll go over my negative comments first to help temper expectations about this game.
[list]
[*]There is no way to change your difficulty once you've selected it, short of starting an entirely new game. I had selected the Veteran difficulty (which is the hardest one short of permadeath), and by the time I reached the first boss I had realized that I wasn't having fun on the difficulty that I'd chosen, but I was too far in to consider starting over.
[*]The game doesn't give you very many options to approach combat, especially in the beginning of the game. Most weapons are slow, and even the faster weapons don't feel super fast. Trying to attack in midair will kill your momentum, preventing you from moving forward or backward, and there's no way to cancel an attack once the animation has started. Once you've built a collection of various weapons, shields and spells, you have a bit more freedom for approaching combat, but most enemies still feel like there's a "correct" way to beat them, and any other strategy will typically fail. This makes combat feel more like a puzzle than an action game, which does have its own merits, but if that isn't what you're expecting you're likely to be dissapointed.
[*]While the game doesn't refresh your health and mana at the warp/save points on the map, it is actually pretty easy to refill those resources safely from an early point in the game (before the first boss). Once you get the Purifier, you can just refresh your health by standing in water and refresh your mana by going a couple spaces to the left of the first warp point. I don't understand why the devs didn't just let you regain max HP/MP at the save points when you still effectively can, it's just a bit more of a pain to do so by using the warp points.
[*]While the game gives you plenty of options for keeping your health up, the game gives you almost no ways to interact with your MP till past halfway through the game without using consumable items, which are either rare or expensive. This makes magic spells feel like a resource that's "too good" to use, especially with your limited mana pool that doesn't increase until you're close to done with the game.
[*]Gold is very hard to come by for the most part. Most of your gold will come from selling your old equipment as you replace it, meaning that you won't be able to buy a whole lot until the later parts of the game when you have a lot of spare equipment to pawn off.
[*]Potential quest spoiler here: [spoiler] A lot of the games rewards for solving puzzles or exploring the map are tied to the golden treasure chests, and before you have the chance to open any of them you receive a quest that SPECIFICALLY states that you can't open any of them. This quest doesn't complete until almost the end of the game, so if you're aiming for the 100% run you'll be left finding chests you can't touch, which isn't a good feeling. [/spoiler]
[*] Definite story spoilers: [spoiler] The "big twist" that the game tries to pull is foreshadowed so heavily that it's obvious from nearly the beginning of the game. The game keeps slamming this foreshadowing at you with almost every story-required dialogue in the entire game, making the so-called twist feel much less impactful and more like a foregone conclusion. I wish it was more subtle so that I could have that "Oh, this is what it all lead to" moment, or actually feel smart about uncovering the plot ahead of time. [/spoiler]
[/list]

Now that that's out of the way, let's talk about the things I like about the game
[list]
[*]As stated earlier, the game's story is actually a lot of fun to delve into. Since the game brings you in with no knowledge, it's really engaging to slowly uncover more about the world as you play through it, learning what happened to its inhabitants as you explore the various areas.
[*]The aesthetics of this game are on point. There's a ton of different areas to explore, each with a theme that all the enemies, objects, and music match. It helps the game feel varied as you continue to explore the world, and keep you immersed in the experience.
[*]The actual exploration of the game feels great. The game will often connect old areas to new ones, giving you access to treasures that were just out of reach or shortcuts to move between zones more quickly. There's not a whole lot of hidden areas, but there's enough to keep you engaged as you explore, checking your map to see how the zones connect to figure out how to get your hands on that treasure you can see just past that door.
[*]The artwork in the game is fantastic, both the pixel art that the actual game uses and the portraits you see in dialogue. There's an entire gallery with even more art you can unlock, and a fair amount of the art is available from the start of the game as well.
[*]While a full playthrough only lasted me around 8 hours, this game has quite a bit of replayability. Beating the game unlocks three new game modes, all with new ways to play. Two of the game modes modify the heroine in some way, but the other game mode actually expands the storyline by letting you play as 3 of the other characters in the game, and is incredibly unique (and possibly the most fun).
[*]The devs put a lot of thought into the elemental reactions, and how your equipment can interact with them. For example, using lightning in water will carry the spell through the entire body of water, or you can poison water to make anything in it take damage. There's also a fair number of jars and such you can use to spread oil and poison to interact with. You can give yourself an "unfair advantage" by negating the effects of these on yourself with certain equipment (such as the Purifier making you immune to poison on the ground and in water), allowing you to subject your foes to these hazards with impunity, which can be quite fun.
[/list]

All in all, I rather enjoyed this game in spite of its flaws, and if you enjoy the sidescrolling exploration experience, I believe you will to.

There's not a Metroidvania in recent memory that I've enjoyed as much as Lost Ruins. Blasphemous is a little tight for me personally, and Dead cells relied too much on random chance and grinding to really experiment with "the" set I would decide I want to use.

Lost Ruins achieves what both of those systems went a little overboard to really do. The combat is tight crisp, but not in a way that punishes you for not reacting in 0.2 seconds, and the equipment system allows you to experiment with what you want to do without the worry of losing it all. 

A lot of people say that the game encourages you to cheese it, and I cannot stress this enough. When I found the combination of spells types and items I beat the final boss with just over a little more than halfway into the game, I could've sworn I'd found an exploit. And I'm confident that in any other game, it would've been. In Lost Ruins, however, I found that I'd only begun what that particular build was, eventually finding multiple upgrades to it that completed the kit and turned me into a professional buzzsaw impersonator by the end of the game. The best part about it? It was sub-optimal for most situations. There's no all-round "good" build, or perfect meta. Some are better than others, yes, but some flourish in situations that others flounder in.

Lost ruins is a Metroidvania with no direct upgrades or "You can now magically double jump" powerups, only sidegrades. You can run straight to the first boss without much hassle, but it'll probably kick your trash if you don't have either the item that lets you move freely in it's arena or the item that [i]actively heals you for existing[/i] on the type of floor the boss arena is covered in. Nothing makes the game itself free, but plenty of things can make specific situations free, or pretty close if you puzzle out how what you're dealing with interacts with what you're using. Using a life drain spell as a crutch? Better find something else if you're dealing with skeletons that don't have any life to drain. 

The main criticism I see of this game is that "you swing slow". That's done intentionally. Most of the enemies in the game have [b]very[/b] simple (read: the same, single attack) patterns, allowing you to hit them if you plan around it, and learn when to swing. Hell, I did a lot of the game with the 2-handed greatsword who's absurd damage output was only matched by it's range and time it took to swing. Lost Ruins isn't so much a twitchy fast-paced combat like Dead Cells or Blasphemous, and trying to talk shit to enemies like it is will hit you with a rather steep difficulty curve. Not an impossible one, but one that's more bullshit than genuine learning, especially early on.

Sadly, it is fairly short. I've finished the main game on the recommended difficulty and the "boss mode" campaign in only 9 hours, but I do see myself coming back to this game still for the harder difficulties and to poke around in new playstyles to see what else I can make busted. Speaking of, here's my personal recipe: [spoiler]Any summon orb spell + Best Friend = GG. If you finagle your position right, you get more mana back than you used to cast it. Once you've got that down, just sprinkle in Amulet of magic (more orbs) and HP Absorption orb to taste. Everything else is up to you, especially if you're playing on assisted.[/spoiler]

Overall, Lost Ruins is a nice case study in the art of sidegrades. There's always something else for you to try, with the only thing stopping you from blasting to the end of it all being your build-solving skills and how well you can put them into practice.

This is a Korean metroidvania with a monster girl theme and some survival/ryona undertones.

The game has beautiful visuals, with smooth and detailed pixel art animations, as well as slick and sexy character portraits. It's worth getting just for the art alone, but the gameplay is also very enjoyable, provided you don't mind a challenge.

For whatever reason, the trope of a cute high school girl being put in some extreme life-and-death situation is very popular in Korea, and this game is no exception. The combat is difficult, the protagonist is slow and clumsy, even the fastest weapons take a bit to wind up, and you have to commit to animations. Moreover, there are numerous status effects, you can be poisoned, electrified, frostbitten, lacerated, set on fire etc etc. Suffice to say, it's very easy to die in just a few seconds. An enemy spits some poisonous liquid on the ground, your overhead swing catches a light fixture, and boom, the room is on fire and you're rapidly losing HP unless you can stop the burning status. It sounds awful, but it's actually very fun and to be honest quite refreshing compared to all those cookie cutter metroidvanias where you just zip around the map spamming attack mindlessly.

Having said that, while the game is punishing, it's not meant to be frustrating, e.g. the save points are quite common, but they do not restore your HP/MP. Instead you have to rely on consumables, which the game has tons of. Some of them restore HP/MP, others deal with status effects or provide temporary buffs. The environment is very interactive and as a result the combat can be quite creative. For example, the first boss is very difficult to take head on. But the boss arena is filled with shallow water, and you can just equip a rubber swimsuit and spam shock spells for an easy win.

The progression is more similar to [url=store.steampowered.com/app/774361]Blasphemous[/url], as in you don't unlock any new abilities. The initial moveset is exactly what you get, there won't be a double jump upgrade later on. There are no level ups either, you'll be just as fragile by the end of the game. The diversity instead comes from the massive selection of weapons, spells and equipment. You can use knives, axes, swords, bows, hammers, various throwables etc. You can cast an invisibility spell, sneak up on an enemy and execute a sneak attack for an easy one shot with gore chunks flying everywhere.

As for mitigating damage, there's the usual dodge roll as well as shields. Shields block virtually all damage and can stagger smaller opponents, whereas the roll is useful for getting behind enemies and dodging bullet hell patterns during boss fights. Oh, and the game doesn't have any contact damage which is really cool.

Story wise, there's about a dozen NPC questlines, providing both comedy and fanservice. Notably, the Lusty Argonian Maid from [url=store.steampowered.com/app/489830]The Elder Scrolls[/url] makes a guest appearance. The localization is quite decent for a Korean game, the dialog flows naturally, there aren't any typos or mistranslations.

My only nitpick would be the excessive inventory management. Sadly, there's no way to save gear presets (like in [url=store.steampowered.com/app/692850]Bloodstained[/url]), so e.g. switching from a melee build to a bow build would require re-equipping all your gear to respec into ranged damage.

A single playthrough will take about 8 hours, but there are multiple endings, as well as bonus modes. One of the bonus modes lets you play as a trio of characters, just like in [url=store.steampowered.com/app/1018010]Castlevania III[/url].

You could go for quick attacking weapons with bleeds, slower hard hitting weapons, or numerous spellcasting builds to get through the game in any way you see fit.  

Some things are a bit awkward, such as momentum loss when attacking midair, but they are all just the rules of the world you abide by to get through.  The writing and humour is charming, and the story itself is simple but fun to experience.

Would recommend this game.  It has lots of replayability as well, with different challenge modes unlocking by completing the first run of the game, as well as multiple endings depending on how you do things.

Without elaborating much, the only real complaint I didn't already know I was going to have coming into this game was the magic system.  There are equippable accessories that give you constant MP regen you find very late in the game.  Otherwise, your MP NEVER regenerates at all unless you use restorative items which tend to be expensive to buy and somewhat rare to pick up.  The basic (lousy) spells give you up to 4 casts to exhaust your entire magic bar, and the useful ones as few as one or two casts. That's it.  The spells are almost all terrible.  Once you've gotten the two accessories that make magic use practical, magic becomes almost overpowered, one shotting just about any enemy and doing around 1/5th of a boss's health bar per charge if you exploit elemental weaknesses. I don't have a quick and easy solution for this problem.  It just feels like the game developers got lost trying to come up with the magic system, and it's not very good as a result.  You find new spells constantly throughout the game, but it never feels practical to use them at all outside of necessity to open a door or something until you find the items that regenerate your MP.  It would have been nice if there was a scaling up system where spells were either much more useful in the early game when casting them was extremely expensive, there was a very slow regeneration of MP by default, or even a system that regenerates MP for killing enemies so that the player would feel welcome to use it offensively. Fun and brief. Worth picking up on sale, for sure. I finished my first playthrough on hard mode after just a handful of hours, no guides or breaks needed.

Enemies are varied, but extraordinarily simple. Most have exactly one unique attack; a handful of larger minions have two; bosses have, by and large, three per phase. Their art is well-styled and cohesive. All enemies have tells and consistent AI. The bosses are all young women that embody various fetishes, like slime girls, succubi, and a few other less-decent ones, but only the art plays off of that; the limited conversations and lore are completely nonsexual (with the exception of one comedic quest giver who exists to reference erotica from The Elder Scrolls).

It controls like a classic post-SotN Castlevania game, with a few exceptions. The most notable is that swinging a weapon cancels all sideways momentum and controls. Startup and end lag is significant on most weapons, and you'll have to learn how to approach and disengage from each enemy individually. Back dashes are replaced with a Souls-like dodge with very forgiving i-frames and infinite uses.

While I've heard complaints about the combat feeling slow or unwieldy, I enjoyed it. Some enemies or bosses are fast enough to swing twice before the slowest weapons can swing once, but they're rare. (Plus, slow weapons are going to be the least flexible -- why should you be able to tackle every threat that exists using only a greatsword?)

While this game is tagged as a Metroidvania, you don't collect new movement options, there are no secretly-breakable walls, and the game is entirely linear with no necessary backtracking. Attack options (weapons and spells) are collected or bought throughout the game, including in one-screen optional areas that are barely hidden. Puzzles are simple and small.

The developers also describe the game as "survival", but I disagree. Free, unlimited, unconditional regeneration is available before the first boss (for a toggleable penalty to max HP that you can switch off once you're healed), there's a checkpoint every third or fourth screen, and unless you choose the permadeath difficulty, you can simply treat the consumables as you always do: as things to be hoarded and unused.

Lastly, I very much like the flexibility offered by the environment. Acid on the ground will poison you, but if you light it on fire, it will burn anything that touches it until it's exhausted. Casting ice spells in water will indefinitely chill it to damaging levels for both you and foes. Certain surfaces and regions are "sticky" and slow you down. It's all intuitive, and it's neither over- nor under-used.

Overall, heartily recommended. It's a cute fusion of gameplay elements that doesn't overstay its welcome.

[h1]Full Review[/h1]
Lost Ruins was advertised to me as a metroidvania but I never really got that feel. You don't gain new abilities or skills that open up previously inaccessible areas, the game's pretty open from the start and instead relies on puzzles and exploration to unlock new areas. The main idea of the game, is that you're criminally underpowered at the start and really don't know anything about the world. And you don't really learn much by playing: besides some cute and funny dialog, the story is really of no consequence and shouldn't be a reason to grab the game. 

It's a hard game, but only really near the start. From the beginning to the first boss, you'll struggle to make progress as you only have one equipment slot and your equipment selection is slim. Enemies hit hard and you lack many means to heal. After the first boss but before the second, it gets a lot easier, especially since you gain an extra equipment slot and can get a passive heal equipment. Shortly after you get a passive magic point regen item which is where the game starts to become trivial.

Some of the later bosses I could do on first try without any difficulty because the tools at your disposal are so plentiful and powerful when paired with passive HP/MP regen: it's difficult to lose. Even the final boss, you could stand still and just regen and use up curatives to stay alive and deal damage without need for dodging or evading attacks. It really does get that easy.

You have many weapons, spells, and equipment to choose from, but it's clear from the very start that speed is the name of the game, as enemies will stagger or be pushed back when hit. All enemies I could find could be stun locked, although the window for some of them is very slim, like the skeletons with shields. For the whole game I used daggers and a shield, and the shield honestly wasn't necessary. Using swords or hammers can be fun, but it's way too slow to really be effective unfortunately. But that's the whole shtick of the game, that attacks take time and need to be timed as an exercise of risk vs. reward.

The soundtrack is quite nice. It's very muted, subdued, but very effective in setting tone. Each of the world's locations have their own track which repeats, but it's seamless and fits the locations well. The sound design in general is very nice: I noticed if I was on the left side of the screen, audio from my left speaker was more pronounced, being able to hear water dripping or footsteps clearer, and as I moved to the right side of the screen, the sound traveled with me, migrating to the right speaker. It's a neat use of spatial audio here.

It took me a couple of hours to really get into Lost Ruins but I'm glad I stuck with it. It is extremely challenging in the beginning but you quickly get into the flow of things. I did a couple playthroughs and it took me 9 hours but I was thorough and did some achievement hunting, too. There's additional modes that unlock on game end which give you specific builds or restrictions which can make for interesting second or third playthroughs. I think the value is here, it just might not be for everyone. It's a cute game with clear love in it, but the difficulty can scare some away.

Ssometimes simplicity is what we need when it comes to our game mechanics. Though, we should not misinterpret simple for easy in all senses. Lost ruin is an interesting one for me. I went from liking it to hating it to liking it again. First of all I will touch on individual aspects of the game. 

COMBAT:

This game is definitely one of the more unique metroidvanias that I have played. The combat is best described as slow and methodical. The movement of your character is rather slow as well as the attacks she performs. You basically have to learn an memorise the move and attack patterns of not just bosses but every enemy in the game as well as the distance of your weapons attack to position yourself properly. Also when attacking you are locked in the attack animation, and you can move again after the attack is executed or something interrupts your attack.

The HP you have is extremely low and most enemy attacks do 1/3 or 1/2 of your hp. Combine that with a plethora of damage over time effects that those attacks inflict and you will legit die to 1 hit + the damage over time it comes with it. Hitting enemies with your attacks is also iffy as some do get staggered from getting hit and others do not, so you have to play a guessing game with each new enemy you encounter as to how you have to approach fighting it.

MAP & ART DESIGN:

The map is pretty well designed in my opinion. It is quite interconnected and you have options based on which path you want to take when going forward. Since the game does not have any new abilities the only progression barriers are keys that are scattered around the map and a few boss fights. The map is also full of environmental traps, which would not be that big of an issue, but every one of them inflicts one of those before mentioned damage over time blights which just make them a pain. Also this damage over time thing stacks, lets say you fall into spikes and now you are bleeding for 10s and right after you are hit by an enemy that also causes bleed with their attacks, yo now have a 20s bleed timer under your health bar. 

As far as the art style goes I think it i beautiful. Art is obviously subjective, but if you like pixel art you will definitely like this game. The environments feel real and are full of detail in both foreground and background segments. There are also a few clever cases of environmental story telling, but those cases are rather in-fequent.

STORY (Slight spoilers):

I was personally not that big of a fan of the story of this game. The story is just your generic Isekai plot where a what appears to be a high school girl gets thrown into a new, magical, dungeon like world. Also your character does not even have a name, nor can you name her and her personality is as complex as as a shape puzzle for toddlers. Heck she does not even have a name (nor can you name her), because amnesia. 

You are then tasked by the sorceress Beatrice to defeat the followers of the "Dark Lady" and you proceed to do just that. You meet a few non-boss npcs along the game, but each one just gives you a random quest and a bit of lore about the world. 

BUGS AND FRUSTRATING GAME DESIGN:
While playing I encountered two different bugs. One was that when you rode an elevator upwards if you jumped your character would sometimes clip trough that elevator and fall down to the bottom. A similar thing also happens when you ride an elevator and get hit by an attack. Even if you all on the elevator platform you will fall trough it to the bottom. This is nothing game breaking, but it is kinda annoying.

The second bug I encountered was that your attacks did not hit. Sometimes when your weapon clearly overlapped with the enemy they took no damage, knock back and there was just no indication that an attack landed even though it clearly did visually. On bosses that might have been just the case of them having temporary invincibility and I did not know about it but it also happened with regular enemies, bats in particular.

And now for one of the most frustrating things about this game. Your character can get knock back locked and you have no invincibility frames after you get hit. You know how in some games bosses like to hurl a barrage of attack at you and you have to dodge them, but it is kinda tricky so you will most likely get hit by at least 1 projectile. Well if that happens to you in this game the one projectile that will hit you will knock you into another projectile and that other one will hit you in another one and suddenly you are insta dead, since, like I mentioned before this game has no invincibility frames after getting hit. So if you get hit for example by  This is incredibly frustrating, especially since your only movement option in the game (besides walking) is a dodge roll, which is rather slow, you can not control the distance of how far you roll.

Overall the game is fun and rewarding. You will have to put some more effort into learning and adapting to its mechanics, and learning to deal with the frustrating bits but once you get a hang of it it can be a pretty fun and rewarding experience.

Lost Ruins is a metroidvania that tries to offer combat that rewards throughtful use of tactics and cunning rather than quick reflexes, and though i think it fails in that regard i still think it's an enjoyable game.

The only challenge comes from analyzing a situation and equipping whatever pieces of equipment deals with it. Player creativity is rarely required, mostly exploiting game mechanics. However, since death comes very easily, it still feels good to overcome the obsctacles Lost Ruins presents you with, even though it is usually in spite of its design rather than in tandem with it.

Knowing this, what does the game get right ? simply put, it feels good to play; movement hits a good balance between weighty and responsive and weapons are varied enough to justify switching loadouts often. It's also pleasant to the eyes and ears, with a fitting if forgettable soundtrack and wonderful pixel art. Finally, the story is surprisingly enjoyable: it is self aware and jokey in tone, but the finale adds an unexpected layer of emotion that sends it off nicely.

If you're interested in a metroidvania with slow, almost puzzle like combat, give REDO! a try. I think it succeeds in that regard much better than this game. Otherwise, Lost Ruins is a perfectly fine way to spend 7 hours exploring a good looking world and interacting with a flawed but interesting combat system. 
Some of the game modes you unlock after beating it are also very cool and let you get more bang for your buck.

A really charming game with beautiful, breezy pixel art, lush animation and lighting effects, endearing characters and character portraits, and an enjoyable, fairly mellow soundtrack. The storyline is straightforward and accessible, the finale is satisfying, and overall the game just feels very complete. I really loved the tremendous variety of melee and ranged weaponry, spells, and equipment with powerful and distinct perks - there's a lot more potential for buildcrafting here than you might expect in a typical 2D metroidvania.

Combat can be a bit janky; each speed category of melee/spell attack feels a few shades slower than it should, enemy stagger thresholds are a bit inconsistent, etc. Difficulty and damage scaling occasionally feel off - some negative status effects last way longer than feels necessary and are particularly punishing.

But these are minor annoyances, and ultimately I found they only encouraged me to dig into the game's diverse toolkit for creative solutions to trouble spots. Enemies who spam shields can be overcome with heavy weapons that ignore blocking; flying enemies who are impossible to target can be brought down with auto-strike spells like Chain Lightning; monsters with low stagger points can be crippled with Orb abilities, etc. etc. The game throws a lot at you, but always equips you with the tools to handle it. I found myself constantly switching up my loadout throughout the game's reasonable ~7 hour runtime. It was a great feeling that made for a varied gameplay loop, and I really credit Altari Games for engineering that.

Lost Ruins might not satisfy people looking for a more hardcore experience or snappier combat, but I really enjoyed my time with the game, and definitely recommend it to anyone looking for a quick metroidvania with some gentler anime aesthetics.

For a small team of devs I must say the game is quite fun. It is short but there is some replayability.

THE STORY:
The story is pretty straight forward with some twist and turns here and there which gives is a vague dark souls feeling because nothing is directly told to you and exposition so its fun trying to guess who the big bad is even if its nothing new its refreshing to say the least.

THE ART:
The art style is fun and animated very well. I have no issue with the over-sized pixels as it is more likely an art decision and not a limitation of the dev team. I've seen art styles where the characters have no faces so big pixels should not make or break how the game feels. Its all subjective so if big pixels bother you don't buy it.
With that being said, the big bosses look awesome and are animated gorgeously.

THE GAME PLAY:
There is a learning curve here as to say the game wants you to learn how to play it not apply what you have learned from other platform games like it. The jumping, attacking, dodging, and hit boxes are essentially pixel perfect but they also have what Id like to call real weight to them. First I gotta say that this game has a questionable power progression system that changes heavily based on player choice EX: You start the game with a low damage and meh attack speed that most enemies will straight up hit faster and stun lock you to death if you don't get the drop on them; now, you go from that to press 2 buttons and proceed to tank using your face while watching everything on screen dies and the change is either sudden or a slow power creep dependent on your choice which has a slight spoiler that I will mention near the end of this review.
With that out of the way this game is very smart and it makes you feel smart. Every item has a purpose and exploration is rewarded handsomely. Items goes from basic RPG staples like extra damage and defense > to questionable if used alone > to kill everything without them touching you when combined > and up to self propelled demigod when used correctly EX: there are items that makes you immune to poison, doesn't do much alone but you can turn an entire body of water into a hazard that kills everything in it if you hit it with poison so..... equip the item, hit the water with poison and everything dies while leaving you unscathed. This is one of the many examples of the smart ways to fight that the game actively encourages you to do through seemingly brutal enemies encounters and there are many combinations of equipment, weapons and consumables that can be combined that turns a deadly encounter into a walk through the park and do not feel bad about using them as the game is quite generous with item drops. 
The enemies in this game have quite the variety in how they fight and what they are weak to, which make different areas feels unique and fresh. The bosses in this game are a hit or a miss since whether or not you explore and find items in the area can change the fight from darksouls level to kirby adventure so use your brain for the purpose of min-max cautiously to preserve the experience... I guess. There must be a better way to scale dynamic difficulty in my opinion though this game does it quite well compared to other games that have attempted it.

Now for VERY IMPORTANT and VERY SLIGHT SPOILER and will DRASTICALLY increase your enjoyment of this game if you know about them so I recommend that you keep reading.

At some point you will come across golden chests, these chests contain highly useful items that make the game's power progression feels drastically better and more fun to play BUT, right before you do the game will recommend that you do not open them while giving you vague reasons to do so. Here's the spoiler: the condition is that if you reach nearly the end of the game without opening a single golden chest, at which point the game will tell you that it is OK to open the chests now. After the grueling experience, you will be granted a "good ending" though to be honest all endings feels the same in terms of whether it makes you happy or sad, which is mostly happy-ish, though I would argue the "bad ending" feels better.

So I recommend that you open every golden chest you can find and you will love this game as opposed to torturous beginnings, fun mid game and suddenly I'm playing Animal crossing with but with bloody ritual sacrifice with my enemies on the altar the end.

TLDR: Fun. Niche because require brain usage, rewarding when brain is used, rewarding when explorations are made. OPEN EVERY GOLDEN CHEST. GG.

I wont give a super in depth review on much of the actual game mechanics, but I can give you a bit of my emotional journey starting with this:
If you do not already have experience in games like this, do not play on the hard difficulty. (unless you may be a secret video games masochist?)

Coming into this, I had never played a game like this before, but I did a quick google on difficulty and found the "true ending" is locked behind the hard difficulty, so I started a run on just that. I didn't expect it to be too bad, but damage thresholds are one hell of a thing. So many one shot kills... I think I died a little under 10 times during the tutorial section of the game.

I got hard stuck about 2 and a half hours into the game on the giant slime boss (just long enough for sunk cost fallacy to not restart the game on an easier difficulty), and tried (unsuccessfully) editing my save file to the regular difficulty for about 20 minutes. Because of this, I had to just keep trying, and I tried and tried to "Get good." Eventually, there was a moment of clarity, my skills did not get better (at least not at the time, by the end of the game I used literally the starting sword with generic damage buffs in one final blaze of glory), but I did remember the very first thing this game tells you when you press start. 

"This is a survival game." As it turns out, trying to get good was the problem. The entire first two phases of the boss are just a puzzle with an incredibly simple solution. Hint: Consider the implications of your item descriptions, and don't shy away from using magic, even if it's impossible to regenerate early game outside of consumables.

After solving the "puzzle" the first and second phase was me pressing a single button about 6 times. And from what I can tell? That was the correct way to beat the boss. Like, they said "This is a survival game," I solved the puzzle on surviving the boss. That's what combat in this game is like. The tools they give you can trivialize large portions of the game when used cleverly, as the developers intended.

I'm going on a tangent now, but like really, the hard mode was so hard what the fuck man. I died 126 times to beat the game. I probably enjoyed the game more because I played it on what was basically a fucking challenge run (hardest difficulty and no opening chests for an optional quest that only affects the games ending, despite chests containing all the good early game items, as well as some of the best items in the game), but if I was even a little bit less motivated I'd have quit the game 5 times over.

Despite the fact that the difficulty often felt like "hard but fuck you" instead of "hard but fair" whenever I didn't understand what the game wanted (make clever builds with in game tools to abuse enemy weaknesses and play it safe), I can't help but give this a positive review. It was damn fun, but devs what the hell man. I think some of my hairs went grey when I played this game.

Let me start this off by stating one key detail about this game: It is not, by any means, a metroidvania nor souls-like - although the tags and some online reviews may suggest it is. It's best described as a 2D survival sidescroller with RPG elements. I originally wrote a negative review, but the sole reason for that was because I judged it from a metroidvania point of view.

I really love the artwork, OST, sound-design, dialogue and characters (Sigh... yes, booba included). The gameplay mechanics, however, are quite clunky to say the least. Stationary attacks, no combos, lackluster movement and way too much menuing (ESPECIALLY if you're using magic). The shield literally breaks some of the bosses and so do the invisibility options. Playing without the shield, however, is near impossible when you're up against multiple enemies because the mechanics are too slow to allow you to have any sort of control.

The boss fights are nothing spectacular although still fun (except for Rosie, I hate Rosie and the fact that her entire phase 1 is irrelevant due to shields while phase 2 is bugged in the sense that her jump attack deals contact damage while she's still on the ground/preparing to jump). Generally speaking, the game is somewhat challenging on veteran difficulty - IF you're reckless, that is. The devs reward a methodical approach and if you use everything you have at your disposal, then you shouldn't have too hard of a time. Some of the items have really cool synergies, too.

Now, let's get to the main question at hand: Would I recommend "Lost Ruins"?

It depends. If you're the type of player who values fluid gameplay and a good combat system... No. If you can look past that, then I'd give it a shot. 16€ is somewhat high for such a short playtime, but it makes sense when you see the pixel art and artworks.

Overall I liked the game.
Clearing quests helps a lot with sustainability of HP and MP (f.e. that one bunny-like weapon, that regenerates MP when you hit it).
Gameplay-wise it is entertaining. Encouters may be challenging depending on how quick you adapt to each new type of enemy and boss. Visuals are pleasant to the eye, that is if you don't mind pixelated anime-like style. I also enjoyed some of the OSTs throughout the game.

tl;dr Great metroidvania that even if it's somewhat short, has good survival mechanics that tests the player's creativity and skills.

Lost Ruins, even though it's a metroidvania, it's sold as a survival experience, and as such, it should be tackled with a bit of patience. I see some people complaining about how the combat is slow, heavy and clunky, but I personally like it because you can feel the weight of the weapon you're trying to use, and it was done purposely so you build your character around such "flaws", like equipping a accessory that increases the attack speed of heavy weapons, or cast speed and/or cost of spells, and the game gives the player freedom to do any kind of build, as long you have the equipment to make it work. Early on that might be a problem tho, since you have to either buy the equipment or find it around the map.

You can't grind out of any situation in the game or increases the stats of your character through items, like other games in the genre do, because it doesn't have a level up system, but the game has lots of checkpoints and save points, so it doesn't ending up being too frustrating and whatnot. I personally think there's way too many checkpoints in the game tho. 

I just think that the existence of shields somewhat broke the difficulty down a lot, which enables you to defend yourself virtually against anything, but it's not just aimlessly guarding, since you have to time the guard action correctly to defend (which has a pretty forgivable timing window), and elemental attacks usually pierce the shield (which you can mitigate or nullify completely with the right accessory), so it involves a bit of skill.

Visual wise, Lost Ruins is beautiful. Every area has its own design and particularities, and the use of simulated pixels it's a shown of its own. I like how there's no reuse of enemy design, and how each enemy race suits the area which you encounter them perfectly, without feeling like out of place. The boss design is superb. A bit fanservicey, but it's great. I really like it.

Replay wise, it offers quite a bit of content actually. The main campaign, which is divided into 4 difficulty modes, has two endings, and 3 extra modes are unlocked after finishing it for the first time, which may not contain anything new per se, it offers diversified gameplay and more challenges.

Anyway, I really recommend Lost Ruins to the fans of the metroidvania genre. It may be somewhat slower early on, but keep pushing. It's really fun. It really is what I've expected, and a bit more.

Lost Ruins is a bit of a mold-breaker. It's a metroidvania, but it's not at all about fluid movement or interconnected backtracks or rpg-style progression. It's slow and weighty. Your hitpoints melt in just a few attacks. You have no i-frames on hit, and can get juggled by single attack strings from bosses. You swap your gear frequently, but few items are strict upgrades---just situationally relevant sidegrades.

The tone is almost closer to survival horror, with a focus on resource management and proper equipment, except the game is so punishing that you sort of have to cheese it to win.

Unlike other metroidvanias, which have added a souls style stamina bar as a way to manage attack pressure, Lost Ruins just makes its attack times long. You hit your attack, freeze in place, your animation slowly begins, and if you're lucky and your spacing was perfect and the enemy doesn't suddenly shuffle a pace to the left, then your attack lands.

There's ways you can mitigate this, but even the fastest weapons feel slow. Spells take forever. Dodges have a few warmup frames during which you're not invulnerable, and a bunch of similar cooldown frames at the end. A lot of the time you have to dodge before an attack starts, not as it starts, which makes the dodge sort of useless as an evasion tool instead of a spacing one.

Despite all of this---and despite the fact that I went in expecting Momodora and got this instead---I genuinely liked the game.

It's got a lot that could put people off. Between the slow controls, the extremely dark story, and the weirdly voyeuristic "defeat a boss and gather their underwear" progression, I can't fault anyone for bouncing off it. But the difficulty was satisfying, and learning to cheese the game's mechanics felt fun.

If you're willing to try a slower-paced survival platformer and don't mind a probably-too-much-anime aesthetic, give this a shot.

Also, despite what some online stuff is saying, you can get a good ending without doing a hardcore no deaths run. There's a tiny bit more context that the hardcore no deaths run gives you, but it's like two frames of animation. Just follow the obvious instructions that the unlikeable character gives you and you'll be fine.
