In this action adventure we play a young girl who has been teleported to a castle. In the process, we have completely lost our memory. The castle is full of skeletons of other people who, according to the messages on their cell phones (with rather long-running batteries...), seem to have been teleported to this world just like us and tried (unsuccessfully) to find a way out. Besides goblins and aggresive animals that want to kill us, we also meet the sorceress Beatrice in the castle, who helps us find our way around. Soon we cross a fantasy realm full of monsters and hard-to-conquer bosses to find out how to get back to our old world.

Lost Ruins is a 2D action adventure game in pixel style, in which we can attack our enemies with a variety of swords, axes and other medieval weapons. Soon we'll also learn spells to burn enemies or heal ourselves. The game teaches us to use the environment to achieve our objectives. Flammable liquids burst into flames when they come into contact with burning lanterns or fireballs, ice magic freezes waters. The game's focus is less on frantic jumping passages and more on combat and managing life,magic points, and our inventory. 

[u][b] Conclusion:[/b][/u]
Cute characters, fluid movement animations, lots of items to collect (clothes, food, weapons, spells), an automatically drawn map and portals for fast travel make Lost Ruins a fantastic 2D action adventure.

In accessibility mode you're granted a relic at the start which heals 1 HP every few seconds, reduces enemy health and damage by 25%, gives you an extra item slot (VERY USEFUL), recovers your HP/MP at save points, and prevents bleed, fire, and poison damage from stacking. It amuses me how many people are complaining that a schoolgirl can't swing a broadsword faster than a battle-hardened orc.

That aside, here are some things you need to know:

-- This ain't your daddy's Metroidvania. It's tough as nails and will torture you if you're expecting a mash-happy slash-fest.

-- Combat is clunky and messy, and it's by design. It's supposed to be punishing and brutal, and it's entirely fine if you avoid it. 

-- Even if you avoid combat, you're still gonna die a lot. Poison, bleeding, freezing, and being set on fire will kill you faster and more often than an axe to the noggin will.

-- Recovery items are sparse. If you do find any, this game is a hoarder's worst nightmare, as most fights you get into in the early game will force you to use something. Don't think you can rely on checkpoints to get your HP/MP back either! 

-- Money is hard to get at first (I often got it by selling items). There are lots of items, spells, and weapons to buy but you won't be able to afford many of them at first. Recovery items are a luxury. If you want them, you must sacrifice things to be able to buy them. 

-- The game really makes you think about what items you're equipping. You won't have an all-purpose build. You need to think about what enemies you're going up against and plan accordingly.

-- Graphically, this is one of the most gorgeous games you'll ever play. Truly enchanting pixel art.

-- If I had a complaint, it'd be that I'd like to be able to refresh checkpoints with updated equipment. Checkpoints only become usable again after every third one you activate, and if I die at a boss with the wrong equipment loadout I have to keep remembering to switch to something else each time I die.

edit: I was asked about time to completion. There's a good bit of content in this game. It'll take you probably 8-10 hours on your first playthrough, and then you unlock three (yes, three) new gameplay modes, each with a different way to play the game.

Lost Ruins is a classic dungeon crawl. The controls are clunky, which perfect encapsulates the idea of being a stupid high school girl swinging a zweihander around. However, the clunky controls are likely the biggest hurdle, and in my opinion they warp what seems like an action game into a strategic one. There are many weapons to choose from, all of which halt your momentum when you use them, forcing you to take it slow. If slow isn't your style, this probably isn't the game for you. You can also lobotimize yourself and make the game a cakewalk by using spells and exploiting weaknesses; there's nothing quite like fighting the first boss, getting annihilated, taking a step back and thinking about the nature of the boss and the arena, and then cheesing the boss to death by abusing the hell out of elemental combinations. This is replicated for most bosses, and even sitatuations, you don't have to bash your skull in and just "get gud", there's different strategies to try, and I managed to make the game a cakewalk before the halfway mark just by minmaxing my stats to godhood. Truly euphoric.

The artstyle... look, let's not beat around the bush. It's anime, monster girls, and the like. I can't even pretend to do the "horny" joke, because I'm not a huge fan of the genre, but I will admit the farther along I got, the more tolerable, and even enjoyable the artwork became. This is a discussion on the artwork, as in still frames, if we're talking about pixel work, dear lord it's amazing. The Japanese anime thing might not be a selling point for some, but it's undeniable that if it could be done justice, they have gone above and beyond. You can tell that Altari Games really care about the game they made here.

So, after having no lifed the game and nearly completed all modes, I can say this game is pretty dang good. I do have some minor gripes with it; for example, I was looking forward to the idea of unlockable characters after the game, and while I did get that, it wasn't really the length I was hoping. Again, what you get it well worth it, I just wish after playing all the modes there was more here, a compliment if anything, and a testament to my enjoyment of the game. Also the story is... not great. It's serviceable, but don't get this game if you want a branching story. The game seems to do best when it does the story of: "small snippets of messages left behind, you fill in the blanks" kind of story telling, the main story itself is nothing to write home about.

Finally, this isn't a particularly long game. Once you figure out what works, the game is going to start breezing, or at least it did for me. Still, with the alternate game types you'll get around 10 hours or so, and even still something you could always boot back up to mindlessly play in the background once you've mastered it. Great game, would recommend, Witch mode is busted.

There's virtually no ability gating.  Some treasures are locked behind abilities but the whole map is accessible without any extra abilities.

My biggest gripe is that free Healing is virtually non-existent.  When you die you are teleported back to the last save point with the amount of HP you had when you saved.  so if you saved with 1 HP, you're SOL until you find food to heal with. 
 Healing potions are expensive and the a lot of the food that drops  applies healing over time so in the middle of combat it's not usually viable.  The best way I found to heal for free was to equip the purifier and stand in the water at one of the portals you find.  But even then it's only 1HP/sec so you'll be standing for at most 40ish seconds for a full heal.  Once you get the staff, MP becomes a lot more manageable too.

Overall I give this a 6.5/10.  Good platforming soulslike, bad metroidvania.

Let’s start by stating some key details about this game: Unlike most of the 2D games I’ve recently seen, this is not a rogue-like game, but it is an excellent Metroidvania. Lost Ruins is not as innovative for the genre as others like Hollow Knight, but it masters what it tries to be while being a fun experience.

   - The Combat: Personally, it doesn't feel as clunky as other reviews pointed out. There is a wide variety of weapons, spells, and relics that, sure enough, if you choose right, may trivialize some of the end-game content; and although simple, due to the high variety of enemies and ways to face them, it feels very satisfying sometimes, even needing to change all your equipment mid-battle. There are no death penalties unless it has been far too long since the last save point or if the player tries the Hardcore Mode. Something that really stood out for me is that Lost Ruins does not have contact damage with the enemies! You are not going to die because an enemy touches you; you’re going to die because they attack you.   

  - The Story: I had fun with it, it was okay; most people may call it generic. However, it always appears when you think you are tired of exploring or fighting, giving you time to rest precisely when needed. There are three endings to the regular story and one more for the Boss Mode. Additionally, if you read the notes and do the Boss Mode, you may appreciate the story more.

  - Exploration and Sidequests: The world is not that big, but it has something in every part of it. Most of the sidequests you will clear just by playing, but some almost change entirely how you play the game, such as the quest where you can’t open any chest until the very end of the game. There are some puzzles to solve, and although simple, some are very fun.
Boss and Enemies: every enemy feels unique, and the bosses are very cool to see their gimmicks. There is not much I can say other than go experience it, but there are some special things worth noting that I will be explaining in the game modes section.

  - Game Modes: When you start the game, you have four difficulties. The first 3 are just difficult sliders such as HP and damage, and the other is the Hardcore Mode, where not only the enemies are stronger, but if you die, your save is deleted, and you have to start again from the beginning. Due to the difficulty presented at Hardcore, you will be forced to learn the mechanics the game offers to you as the player and the enemies, resulting in the need for a well-thought-out strategy. In addition to these four base game modes, after you clear the game on any difficulty, you gain three new modes: Assassin Mode, Witch Mode, and Boss Mode. I recommend the first two for players who want to test a new play style of the base game at its best. As for Boss Mode, it is an extension of the story where you play as 3 of the game's main bosses, making you understand their gimmicks while having more story and game to go for.
    
-    In general, I had an excellent experience with Lost Ruins, even going for the platinum. The game is simple, and it doesn't really try to innovate, But what it does is master that simplicity in a way that I’ve never seen before, creating a good time for both casual and experienced players.

Lost Ruins is an interesting Metoridvania. It's slow paced and heavily gear focused. There's not as much focus on dodging attacks as there is building your gear the correct way for a fight. There are also additional modes that can be played. The main game is ~7 hours. Each subsequent playthrough tends to be shorter, as you know what works.

The Good:

- good aesthetic/effects
- cool weapons
- variety in how to play
- well animated/designed bosses
- music
- Assassin Mode is a blast
- Spells interact with the world.
- If you want to, you can break the game (Oil spell plus+4 fire damage makes a fiery oil ball).

The just okay:

- Witch Mode
- Weapon selection
- Has a story
- Bosses need more variety in design. "Giant Waifu" only goes so far

The Bad:

- Boss Mode (feels like you're playing 3 pretty crappy characters)
- Waiting for stuff to refill (MP/HP)
- Inverse Difficulty curve. As you play, you get gear. Gear lets you defeat bosses easier. So, the first boss tends to be the roughest (or the ice one if you're unprepared).
- Good ending locked behind hard mode and doing things a certain way (or so I hear).

Good example of a very fun game with a thousand flaws.

The characters and bosses are all very stylish and the whole thing is a joy to look at.  The plot is predictable and not very memorable but it stands fine without it.  Exploring is a lot of fun due to the wild assortment of weapons, items, and accessories you can find.  You'll never feel like the game is wasting your time, because often what you'll discover is extremely useful for what is up ahead.  The huge assortment of practical collectibles and boss rewards gives a real sense of wonder and adds a lot of variety.

The downside to this is that it leads to a lot of menuing.  When you have a hundred weapons and accessories with specific uses, you'll feel obligated to swap them constantly to be gaining full advantage.  There is no restriction on this, meaning you can literally hit an enemy with a DPS setup and then swap to a defensive one during an attack phase.  It slows the gameplay to a crawl.

Additionally, there is a real problem with the combat in this game, in that weapon speed is far too overpowered.  The increased action delay on using a heavy weapon leaves you wide open, often getting your attacks interrupted completely since enemies tend to attack quickly.  Due to your very low health pool and relatively limited consumables, this is disastrous.  On top of this, faster weapons are better dps anyway, and you can often just stagger enemies and use your shield and counter, rather than trying to secure a larger opening.  It often feels like the optimal strategy is to force a boss into a corner and dagger them to death while spamming food.  The spell to slow projectiles also completely breaks half the bosses.

I should mention that upon completing the game, you unlock a game mode that removes weapons entirely and gives you a Castlevania 3 (or more recently, Curse of the Moon) setup with well-defined characters you swap between.  This actually removes the issue of having to menu weapons, and since the combat didn't make good use of the weapon selection anyway,  the game just feels much smoother.  Menuing accessories and food is still a problem, but it's better.  I wish that the game had been built with this as the main mode instead.

Despite all of this, the game is just fun.  

A thorough playthrough probably runs 10 hours or so, but boss mode was fun enough for me to sink in another several.

Scaling: The game starts out quite hard, but then gets relatively easy. The hp scaling of enemies is too flat. While you can still die from a single enemy, the regular enemy battles are still pretty quick. 

Weapons/Spells: I like the variety. There's a multitude of ways you can get through the game after you've run the past the first area. However, there are significant issues the speed variation in the weapons make many weapons next to useless unless you really like handicapping yourself to hone your skills. The enemy reactions make many slower weapons unusable.  While it's intended that you use specific weapons/spells for different areas of the game, you can eventually cheese through with 3 or 4 after the first half of the game, especially if you pick ranged weapons. 

Bosses: I do like most of the bosses, and definitely died the first try on most phases, but felt some satisfaction in getting the timing down. It's weird that they have the order of the items from the bosses that they do. 

It definitely could have done with more balancing, but was still worth playing.

Lost Ruins is an excellent metroidvania, side scroller game.  Now this is the part where I talk about the story a little bit, but this is one of those games that talking about the story may spoil it for you so I'll just say it's about a young girl who has been teleported into a strange castle.

Okay then the likes, the story is really good at first I thought it was your simple stop the bad guy story but had plenty of twists and turns and well-written characters that just made the story phenomenal, especially when you play the game a second time and everything in the story just seems to click together.

The gameplay is really good it has a bit of a Dark Souls like feel to it, but with metroidvania-styled gameplay, it's tough but fair and when you die it is mostly your fault. It also has a nice balance of weapons and spells you can play with, you can also customize your character with different items to give them more strength or more durability or certain abilities. The weapons and spells are really good each one with their own unique look and power, some weapons and spells are better than others so this game gives incentive to mix and match to figure out which character build works for you. 

The pixel graphics are really beautiful, very well done with plenty of detail and nice little touches to it, I also love the character portraits it has a nice anime feel to it. The levels in the game are really good quite diverse with plenty of interesting locations to look at and explore, like a sewer to a castle to even a crypt, all of it well designed that makes you want to stop and stare at certain places in the level.

The characters are really good very well written even NPC characters with little dialogue are quite interesting. I really like the main character because she's generally a very nice, very caring and considerate person, I also like this demon Merchant she's also really cool character and generally very sweet and caring, also I really like this Dragon maid she's super adorable looking.

The enemies and bosses are really good each one with their own unique design and skill that keeps you on your toes, especially when playing a more harder difficulties. The music is really good with plenty of great tracks to listen to, that fits the game really well especially at the last level.

The game also has quests by certain characters you meet which can give you better weapons or access to areas you couldn't get to before. Now the best things in the game is the multiple endings and different modes to play, basically after you beat the game for the first time you are given different modes like which mode, assassin mode and boss mode both the witch and assassin mode basically makes you play with a certain type of build. While boss mode where you get to play as three bosses you defeated and in that mode we get a completely different story which I found it quite good especially with the interactions of the three bosses. There's also different endings in the game which encourages you to play the game multiple times to get everything.

There's also plenty of great references not just to other video games, but to anime and manga like in one scene it makes references to paper RPGs and berserk. The notes in this game I absolutely love as you know I like notes in video games as it can help build a story and these notes are very good they help build the world; these notes give insight to different characters and the villain of the game.

Okay then the dislikes, alright there is not really anything to dislike about this game, okay there are some things but really they're just so small compared to how great the game is, but here are just some small complaints I have.The platforming can be a little bit frustrating sometimes like you could miss a platform after jumpping even though you were very close to it the platform. The final boss is a bit of a letdown I mean don't get me wrong the final boss has a cool design and she can be a bit tough, but I thought she'd have a second form like all the other bosses but no she doesn't even, not even on more harder difficulties she's still the same, like I said I found that to be a bit underwhelming and a little bit of a letdown.

[h2]Summary[/h2]
[i]Lost Ruins[/i] is a high B-tier metroidvania that marries beautiful simulated pixel graphics with breathtaking particle effects, visually upstaging S-tier [i]La Mulana 2[/i]. The game has consistently funny dialog. It has a depth of accessible and quirky combat options that make fighting monsters endlessly exciting. The map is not complex but it contains interesting areas and a few deceptively simple puzzles. It is a shorter metroidvania; I finished it in 12 hours. If it were longer or if plot twists were less telegraphed, it would easily be an A-tier game.
 
[h2]Pros[/h2]
[list]
[*]This is one of very few games that does [i]simulated pixel graphics[/i] well. The colors are vibrant, the pixels are chunky, and everything/every character is perfectly animated. The anime cartoon characters and monsters animate like pixel-art cartoons, as they should. The volumetric and particle effects work in mesmerizing combination with this style.

[*]Combat is not usually challenging but you will need to restart some encounters over several times to see if another combination of weapons, spells, and relics will work better. Expect unexpected results. Mixing and matching combinations is almost as much fun as watching the monsters instantly explode when their weaknesses are exploited. Enemies and bosses vary greatly from each other and are fun to fight.

[*]Every line of dialog in the game is funny. The protagonist is a dimwitted but sweet schoolgirl who is basically trapped for unknown reasons in a Castlevania-situation. Her lines when confronted with the silly but demented characters she meets are dumb enough or wholesome enough to make you chuckle.

[*]2 endings, driven by player decisions.
[/list]

[h2]Cons[/h2]
[*]No big, narrative-changing secrets to discover. No secret areas. Only 1 "secret" boss (technically just one of a couple of optional bosses).

[*]You see the "twist" coming as soon as the game starts.

This review is going to make me a hypocrite. But hey, we’re all hypocritical once in a while, right? Oh well, here we go.

This metroidvania is pretty heavy on the “-vania”: there are some really heavy RPG elements that, depending on your level of enjoyment of those mechanics, will make or break this game. Elemental damage and status effects abound here and only the right combination of equipment will make life easier for the player. Depending on the player’s gear, a puddle of oil on the floor can either lead to a quick death to the player or a helpful weapon against any baddies standing in the middle of it. At first, this caused me some really aggravating deaths until I started to get a better grasp of the system. Also, it might be worth noting that the menuing can be a little annoying as the player switches equipment in and out for different obstacles, but all-in-all it’s really fun.

The story is pretty silly, despite some twists here and there. But the characters you meet along the way are pretty great. The psychotic butcher schoolgirl, the zombie fangirls, the katana-wielding goblin slayer: they’re all fantastic. On top of that, the enemies the player faces are memorable as well and each poses a different threat while being vulnerable to different damage types. This game constantly mixes things up and keeps things interesting.

Where this game makes me a hypocrite is that it’s very linear – which is precisely the same reason why I didn’t like [i]Guacamelee 2[/i] and why I didn’t recommend that one. Any real exploration is locked behind sidequests, so if the player isn’t paying attention to those, there is no real reason to roam around the world. On top of that, items needed to complete those quests are marked on the map, eliminating any need to do any real searching. The thing that makes this game more interesting than [i]Guacamelee 2[/i] is that the limited exploration usually leads to a unique piece of equipment or a new spell or something. In [i]Guacamelee 2[/i], exploration lead to either a health pick-up, a stamina pick-up, or (eventually useless) money, and that’s pretty much it. [i]Lost Ruins[/i] does it better, is what I’m trying to say.

In the end, I really had a blast with this game. From the characters, to the maps, to the combat, everything came together to make this one a memorable stand-out. If you’re willing to muscle your way through this often-challenging game, you’re likely to find something you like in here. I know I did!

Cute and fun game but has a very steep learning curve and punishing early game. There are a couple of achievements/endings locked behind playing on "hardcore" mode in which you lose your save file when you die and cannot manually save during the game (autosaves only). There is also an optional quest you have to complete to get an ending that makes the game much harder if you decide to complete it. I don't know if I will come back to the game to complete these.

One playthrough is actually fairly short all things considered, maybe 5-10 hours if you are thorough, and only a couple hours if you speed through. Even so, the various obstacles, items, equipment, and magic that you encounter keep it a fresh experience to the point that no matter how far you get or how many items you have, if you use the wrong ones against the enemies you're fighting, you'll have an impossible time. Similarly, if you choose them well, a fight that seems very difficult will be a walk in the park. Some people have commented that the attack speed on weapons is very slow, but this is also a matter of choosing the right approach for the task at hand.

You'll also unlock a few extra game modes after completing your first playthrough. I haven't tried these yet, but if you really liked your first playthrough this will probably keep things fresh for you and give you a chance to tackle the game from a new approach.
Overall I would recommend this due to the interesting and engaging combat implementation (and some puzzle solving too) plus the cute characters and great artwork. The current price of $20 is definitely as high as I would go on it though. Ideally I think maybe $10-15 is a good price point (and I picked it up on sale myself). Still though, you'll definitely know if it's a game for you within 2 hours of playing, so you might as well give it a try if it looks interesting and refund it if it doesn't end up agreeing with you. A compact and streamlined Metroidvania that boasts style, substance, and exhilarating combat, while suffering from a recurring technical issue.

Positive:
- Sprites are vivacious with fluid animations, pixel art is beautifully designed with vibrant colors, and environments are polychromatic with impressive lighting effects. Visually, the overall presentation is top notch, exhibiting and encompassing a gorgeous array of retro styles and expositions.
- The save system depends on checkpoints and savepoints, allowing for convenient saving and loading opportunities without much time spent on replaying what has already been accomplished in order to reach the point of continuation. In a genre that involves at least some degree of retracing steps, backtracking, and revisiting previously reached areas, this accommodation benefits the player and makes progression more efficient.
- Controls are tight, responsive, and can be executed well within the range of one's expertise. Attacking with melee weapons, launching projectiles, and casting spells are all weighty activities resulting is perceivable impacts against enemies and in noticeable changes within the game world. There are weapon and ability mixtures to fit many playstyles, as well as room for experimentation for those interested in acclimatizing to new methods of attack that are mightily tactile and substantially material.
- Although the arsenal of weapons, equipment, and spells is not extensive, what is available is enjoyable and creates variability in the form of adaptive synergies that are fun to perform at their highest potential. Melee weapons hit enemies with a heft that is tangible as a physical force, chemical reactions are explosive and destructive, and spells epitomize magical dismantlements of their targets. With that said, there are certain combinations of items and equipment that absolutely annihilate foes with weaknesses to those item interactions, making for extremely satisfying combat, but practically negating many of the other items during much of the adventure.
- Crucial to the success of the adventurer, one must be mindful of their weapons' strengths and their opponents' weaknesses, as preparing for fights requires prudent planning and the careful equipping of the most effective blend of items. Carrying the most appropriate consumables for specific areas also necessitates judicious organizing, as one maybe depend on a stock of items for emergency measures. This layer of strategy is a welcome addition to the elements of thrilling action demanding dexterity and cleverness in each and every hostile encounter.
- World map provides easy indications of where one has been, where one can or cannot go, and comprehensible icons that are indicative of several interactive mediums. Because of this, becoming lost or not knowing where to go next, is a nonexistent problem in terms of world navigation and accessibility.
- Almost all environmental puzzles are straightforward and sensible, enticing the player to think about their abilities and the physical attributes of the space, and how to utilize them in cooperation to achieve an end. On the other hand, a few puzzles require too much experimentation of valuable resources, such as magic points or expendable items, in order to solve. This is not a hindrance, per se, since traversing the world will allow for the player to accumulate the necessary experience to eventually understand the puzzle expectations over a natural progression of time through the journey.
- Bosses offer the best and most gratifying fights in the game, combining varied attacks, multiple forms, and diverse tactics. This heterogeneous quality to emergent combats heightens circumstances and promotes situational urgency, in addition to allowing the player to consider alternative methods to choosing equipment, items, and when to use consumables, all in especially consequential moments in the journey.

Neutral:
- Navigating menus can be fiddly, as there are several submenus to use and a map to peruse. This initial discomfort eventually subsides as the player becomes more accustomed to using the appropriate buttons or keys, so it is not a lasting issue. Going to and from the map from another menu can be especially pesky.
- Plot and story involve the findings and interactions of a young girl in the context of an otherworldly setting, including the tropes and generalizations of myriad previously released fantasy narratives, but it manages to be sufficiently entertaining as the flavor to the more important player-controlled branching action platforming adventure. On that premise, the standard of the actual writing is unexpectedly skillful and competent, adhering to proper English grammar expectations, and applying descriptions and expressions that are wholly proficient.
- Most characters present in the game world are female humans and female humanoids that are moderately sexualized, but in a relatively tasteful manner. While some characters certainly demonstrate a proclivity to expose cleavage of the breasts, as well as the choice of donning very tiny articles of clothing, revealing other parts of the anatomy, it is all portrayed playfully, innocently, and unoffendingly, without any innuendo toward pornography. Ultimately, this scantily clad aesthetic is merely cosmetic, and there are never any allusions made to the reasoning behind the fashion choices.
- Beating the game unlocks a few more difficulty modes, which operate under specific restrictions and specifications, along with a total of three endings for the player to attain, and more achievements to unlock, but these variations are not significant or revelatory to warrant multiple playthroughs.
- Mechanics, itemization, and world traversal are neither deep nor complex, with the overarching experiential arrangement being as linear as a Metroidvania could possibly be. Learning battle techniques is clear and nonambiguous, discerning how to best employ items and equipment is uncomplicated, being lost in biomes and areas is a trivial rarity, and finding oneself underpowered against any enemy is not functionally applicable. All facets and aspects of the gameplay are well-defined and transparent, with the primary requisite for triumph being battle alertness and item knowledge.

Negative:
- Crashes happen very frequently, rendering the software unusable, and requiring a manual termination. There seems to be some engine-related glitch that causes the game to sever the connection between graphics and audio, causing the video portion of the software to stop functioning while keeping the rest of the game operable in the background. Ending the application, restarting, and loading a previous save will allow for the maintenance of the problem, with some lost time due to the gap between the save time and the crash time. There have been several posts about this in the discussion forums, but the developers never fixed this major problem.
- Upon starting the game, one must wait through ten seconds of promotional splash screens associated with the engine, developer, and publisher. There is no way to skip these, and their sole purpose is to waste the player's time.

Overall rating: 3.5/5.0

So I got this as part of a Humble Bundle. It's a little pricey in my opinion, but $20 isn't bad for what it is. With the other options out there, I thought it might have been $15.

The graphics are pretty good and things are usually easy to distinguish. As others have noted, a way to switch between two equip sets would have been nice, but once you get used to the game the inventory management really doesn't feel that bad. It's mostly the first playthrough that it feels a bit much. That said, the game reminded me quite a bit of Circle of the Moon, one of my personal favorite Castlevania games so maybe I'm just used to opening up my inventory to switch minor things around.

I will say that once you get into the artifacts and how they affect your weapon swing speed, it honestly kind of hurts the game. Some weapons show up too late to be particularly useful and even "fast" weapons can feel pretty sluggish, so knowing your character's attack speed is pretty important. It makes some weapons kind of superfluous though. And that's kind of what makes the inventory more bearable after you have more experience with the game too: some weapons will just feel better or be able to do better things.

Due to the dev's focus on survival, there are no quick refill points. You either have to spend an artifact slot or weapon slot or eat a consumable. The inventory sorts by newest by default, but it can also be sorted by name, so knowing that is also very helpful towards good inventory management once you understand what items cure or nullify certain effects.

Enemies can be run past or cheesed in various ways (water has several cheesy things you can do to enemies inside while mitigating the effect on  your character through consumables or artifacts). They either drop consumables or pittances of gold, so don't worry about fighting every enemy. 

Bosses are where the combat really comes into play in figuring out patterns, openings, vulnerabilities, and even environmental hazards that you can take advantage of. Most of the bosses have two major phases: a player-sized form and a big form that has its own phases. If you know what you're doing late-game, the bosses with defined phases are pretty easy to cheese, which is kind of good if you want to attempt the Hardcore difficulty.

Overall, it's good and can be beaten in a few hours. Once the game is beaten, you unlock a Castlevania-like boss mode and two modes that focus on spellslinging or crits that really remind me of COTM's extra modes. It's a nice little bonus that changes the way you play without making tons of changes. The major weapons and artifacts with effects that don't make sense for the mode (such as attack speed buffs in Witch Mode) get new effects thematically appropriate to the mode (like a casting speed buff instead) and become either active or passive artifacts instead of normal equips. I'm not kidding about a few hours per playthrough either. I've beaten it four times so far on different modes with only assassin and hardcore left.

So it has balancing issues with its weapons and spells (there are a few absolutely amazing options and a lot of eeehhhh.... ones by comparison). I really wish the default attack speed was faster and didn't stop your forward momentum dead in the air. I also really wish there was some sort of more plentiful healing available that wasn't consumable or equipment based since that partially exacerbates the balance issues. The story isn't going to blow anyone away and it's a little ecchi at times with character designs. The music is balanced pretty low and is fairly lowkey "ambient sense of dread" for most of the game though there are a few nice tracks. 

That said, finding the little tricks to recover health or make certain rooms easier when attempting to collect most of the stuff is still fun. Finding the best boss strategies to balance out your damage and survivability was quite fun, like little puzzles, and environmental effects add a bit more depth that I appreciate. The extra modes add a bit more replayability to the experience as well. It is a little hard to recommend for $20 with its flaws and quirks, but it's a solid game built around map exploration and equipment combos.

Biggest personal peeve has to be the slow respawn time after each death. The game has to finish playing the slow motion death sequence of your player character -  the body hitting the floor, bouncing once, then settling down - before the retry menu comes, which gets a bit aggravating after the first dozen or so time, especially when you just want to get back for a retry again.

There's also the somewhat slow attack speed, but I could get used to it pretty soon so it's really not that big a deal as I feared it would be. 

Other than that it's a fine game, not perfect but something you can pick up and have fun with for a few hours. 

One thing I would say however, is that it's more a metroidvania-lite than a pure metroidvania.

At first I thought this was gonna be some Castlevania/Momodora hybrid but as time went on it started to feel more Shantae. And this is mostly due the writing and the enemy variety which I'm sure has been a huge inspiration.

I'd argue that the early part plays like I mentioned, then turns into Shantae up until you reach the late stage (think clock tower) when it goes back to being your typical Metroidvania because this is when difficultly really ramps up. And like Shantae there is no way to level up, meaning you have to rely on your gear, spells, upgrades and most importantly your wits.

If you know what you're getting yourself into and can deal with the difficulty (spikes) then the game is about 6-8 hours depending on how fast you rush it like skipping achievements or not, going for optimal builds or not. You can definitely do it in half the time if you so choose, but I choose to cheese half the game due to some glaring issues. Did I mention you get the option to cheese your way quite early on? You'd think that wouldn't the case but it is. It's so powerful in fact that it can easily carry you for 80% of the game once you realize it. It's bad game design no doubt considering everything else at your disposal and makes the game quite trivial and boring if you choose to use it. But that's what I did during my first playthrough. 

There's a few issues with spells and certain equipment later on as well which makes the game quite trivial to the point were weapons are kinda useless (other than for achievements). Normally you aren't really expected to be carried by magic often being a limited resource, but you can go ham quite literally if you so choose at a certain point. Often if not always you have to rely on some weapon build but it's kinda pointless and sad considering the arsenal at hand. A missed opportunity for sure. 

As for the the weapons themselves, you'd think they cause staggered damage of some kind in this game, but nope... you have your debuffs and that's it, while it's magic that does everything else. And oddly enough it's the opposite for enemies since they are all mostly melee while having longer range. Technically everything an enemy does will make you stagger and fall through platforms whenever possible.

And now unto said glaring issues if you ask me at least, which can make this quite a bad experience if you aren't prepared, namely:
- Konami/Capcom/Tecmo NES era enemy placement. Although not as bad you can get chain staggered by enemies which can lead to cheap deaths if you're not careful. So plan accordingly (if/when possible).

- Infamous From Software animation locks and delays. I still think this is one of the biggest banes to game design since it crept into everything imaginable where it shouldn't have been in the first place. Weapons and spells in general have an overly long windup time which is slower than the enemy, and even with certain gear it becomes very tedious to the point where you can just match up to the enemy by deflecting them, i.e arrow vs arrow which is just bad game design overall. I'd treat the exploration part more as a stealth game, especially when you have access to spells and health/mana regen. Learn the animation cycles instead of relying on brute force unless you can of course towards the end.

You'd think that after 35 years (Ninja Gaiden) that meleeing certain ranged enemies would be just as easy if not easier, but think again. Thanks to "brilliant" From Garbageware it now is the exact opposite instead. Jumping and stabbing, slashing or even shooting might as well not exist as a feature unless you like 100% vulnerability because potato. 

There are no iframes or forms of block unless you use a shield and then only a shield, because when you attack you are animation locked for that duration regardless if you hit something or not, tried casting a spell or not. You can by no means swap from attacking to blocking (even with a short delay) like in something "modern" like for example Ninja Gaiden from 2004 or Sekiro from 2019 which means that even if you hit an enemy you will mostly likely get staggered even if they die in one hit, because remember, they are faster than you and have longer range. Even older/other metroidvania titles have some form of evade ability like backwards step which was at least useful overall wheras the roll here is only useful for evading certain traps, boss attacks and finding secrets. And the best of all, even if we had that you still wouldn't be able to use it as intended due to said animation locks.

Imagine if this timeline would've gone with Capcom or even Team Ninja instead. I'd love to see a DMC or modern Ninja Gaiden platformer but that'll never happen now. So thanks From Garbageware for making gaming worse once again.

- The checkpoint system is EXTREMELY half-baked. Normal savepoints work as expected but the checkpoints are really bad because you can't run to the same one again after using it, which means if you did a loop of some area (which this game has A LOT of), you now have to travel further, often twice as long (even though we're talking seconds at most (but this adds up over time) just to use the next checkpoint. I'd almost argue they should've been removed or if you can then avoid them until you cleared the area, but then you end up in a catch 42 because you don't know what's ahead until you do which makes said checkpoint useless on your first run, unless you're really struggling or not saving that often..? 

if you're going for a second run on Veteran or any of the Modes then they make a lot more sense because you kinda know what to expect by then, but this is obviously not the case for first time players. If this game was stage-based then I wouldn't have complained but it isn't, it's a metroidvania. And if you have checkpoints you expect them to work all the time.

It's not about being hard or anything but it's very tedious because you might die due to cheap death on the next room, AND EVEN IF YOU PASSED SAID CHECKPOINT, you now have to rerun the entire area even though you passed the checkpoint twice. And since the game has story bits it can mean rerunning the same part a couple of times which happens the closer you get to the midpoint. At least savepoints are placed next to boss rooms like you'd expect unlike some games which makes you rerun the entire thing to waste your time because reasons. Overconfidence can definitely kill your mood for the game if you end up in some deathloop because you're skipping mobs or forget about some traps when skipping about.

To give a better example; time is limited (shocking I know!), so if every death costs about 1min, over time that can be (over) an hour lost simply due to having to rerun the place you just visited. And trust me, this will happen A LOT unless you go at a snails place. In worse games you get punished for simply sneezing because for some reason you can't pause the game whenever which can lead to a death. 
Why pause could exist 35 years ago, because I need to visit the bathroom or anything other urgent at any given point and not now is anyone's guess. Oh but thankfully you can pause whenever unlike some company's insistence on not letting you do so which is somehow a feature and quite widespread because potato? Thanks said company for making gaming worse! And if you think this was a great idea then I have a bridge to sell you.

There's a few other things I'd love to mention but these would fit more unto a guide other than the things I really had to mention here. But for the asking price I still think it's worth it.

Alright, so I wanted to wait a bit before I made this review because while I was going through my first run of the game I was checking the reviews and I wanted to see if I would have a different opinion after beating the game or going through another run. I'll say that even after beating the game for the second time and now currently on witch mode, I still believe this game is just as great as during my first run. To preface this, I played the game on veteran difficulty for my first run and the second run I played was boss rush mode.

I'm going to touch on the art style just a bit, as I think it's already been said enough but it's really good and fits the whole anime style they were going for. So there's not to much to say on the end of art for the game but I will give praise for the sprites and how you're able to get a good feel for the characters. 

Now let's move onto the gameplay, which has had very polarizing out look on it. I gotta say, I haven't had as much fun with a lot of games I've been recently playing in comparison to this game which I've been having a blast on. As I mentioned earlier, I played this game on veteran mode, so it was especially challenging and it caused me to die quite a lot. Though it was really only at the beginning where I felt like some of the deaths was the games part. In the beginning of the game there are a few enemies that have attacks you just can't punish without taking damage if you didn't get the right equipment but it's pretty easy to avoid those enemies. It won't be long until you are able to come back and kill them anyway because those enemies become quite easy to beat once you get either the spells, weapons, and/or artifact to deal with them. That's where the fun comes in, I was able to play the game how I wanted. There are a bunch of kits in the game where you can cheese out the enemies but there's a lot of customization you can go through to fit your playstyle. When I came back to face those difficult enemies, I wasn't trapped using a certain kit because I had other options. Not every customization is going to be good for an area but you will never be limited to just one kit. This is reinforced with the spells in the game around the mid game you're able to get artifacts and a weapon that grants you mana, so you won't have to use mp potions as often. This means you can just go wild with certain spells and have a blast using them. You feel like one of bosses made the game into a bullet hell just use a spell and don't have to worry about the projectiles anymore or maybe you feel like the enemies ranged attacks are going to fast there's a spell for that too.  The only real issue I had with the gameplay and this is more of a personal one is the hitbox for specific weapons like the hatchet and the Cursed Scythe feel very small and inconsistent at times. This was really annoying to deal with as I would lose all my stacks and begin to take bleeding damage when I thought they were in the hitbox for the Cursed Scythe. 

The combat in the game is the reason why I wanted to make this review in the first place. It was really fun doing what I wanted to do, even if it wasn't the most optimal I could still mess around with it. Late game I had a blast using invis with full stacks on cursed scythe and just one shot most enemies. This ties in with what I believe with games like this, if I can do what I want to do and still feel pleasure in doing so then it's a great game. I recommend this game 100% and if I had to give a rating for this game I would definitely give it 4.99/5 stars.

This game has a fantastic atmosphere. Whenever I boot it up, the title screen music just makes me feel like I'm in a dream. The art-style is on point, along with the OST and animations. Some bosses are out-of-this-world beautiful.

The gameplay is very refined. You get to choose from a number of weapons that differ in size, speed and additional effects. Different weapons are not just slightly stronger reskins of each other, they are meaningfully different. I've seen people complain that the swing animation is too slow, but that is not a valid criticism: there are quick weapons with which you can outpace certain opponents, and there are slow weapons, which, granted, can't outpace some enemies but have some other advantage like range or healing or bleed. On top of that you have a bunch of magical spells, items and equipment that can help you deal with foes that do not go down easy to your usual build of choice.

I want to point out separately that there are various ways to bend the environment to one's advantage, be that setting floor on fire or poisoning water. There is a lot of variability to how you can approach any encounter. There are also shields, and magic sticks, and veils and floaty boots and a lot of other stuff. And there are other very curious interactions that you should try and find for yourself.

Exploration is quite good too. You don't have to visit every nook and cranny of the labyrinth to complete the game, but it will let you find: side stroies, interesting puzzles,  special weapons, special enemies and bosses, new scenery.  The game map does not feel empty in the slightest.

The story is nothing special, but I did find it charming. The dialogues communicate the characters'personalities very well and the characters themselves usually have some nuance to them. Reading small pieces of lore lying about and talking to side characters made me feel connected to the world.

The game does not waste your time. Save points are located in a balanced manner, they neither trivialize nor amplify the difficulty, there is a substantial challenge in getting from one save point to another and yet there is never an annoyingly long stretch of no save points.

The game is also filled to the brim with content. After completing it once, you can replay it in hardcore mode or try for a different ending, or play a new story with different mechanic, or play it again with some restrictions. There are also a lot of secrets scattered around and a gallery to view your achievments.

[h2]TL;DR[/h2]
[list]
	[*]Has combat that rewards adapting your equipment to the situation, but swapping equipment becomes increasingly tedious over time.
	[*]Combat animations generally have the proper wind-up, but the main character’s attack feels janky
	[*]Compelling aesthetic; if you like what’s on the store page, you’ll like what’s in-game
	[*]Well paced difficulty on “Recommened” level
	[*]Restart from the last save point or autosave point on death; no “corpse runs”
[/list]
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Introduction[/h2]
  Lost Ruins is a metroidvania with methodical combat that emphasises adapting your equipment and weapons to suit the situation. It introduces small yet meaningful changes to its genre, but the tedious UI hampers its execution.

[h2]Pixel Art and Anime-Style[/h2]
  The most apparent aspect of Lost Ruins is its visuals — a contrast of clean, anime-styled characters in a grimy, somewhat realistic environment. It’s a compelling aesthetic for those who like both styles. With its pretty pixel art and portraits in gameplay and dialogue, if you like what you see on the store page, you’ll like what you see in-game.

[h2]Adequate Animations[/h2]
  Lost Ruins also has adequate character animations overall — both in visual appeal and for gameplay purposes. The main character’s idle animation is incredibly animated, in two senses of the word. Environmental lighting is also subtly animated, giving everything a glow that makes enemies and your character easy to distinguish from the background. Most enemies have the appropriate wind up before they attack, giving you a fair chance to dodge and counterattack all but the fastest enemies.
  However, similar to older metroidvanias, the main character’s attack feels janky. Every weapon has the same overhead swing at a constant speed, based on their speed stat, so there’s a lacking sense of heft in the heavier weapons.

[h2]Interesting Gameplay, but…[/h2]
  In spite of its combat animations, combat is still interesting enough to engage in. While the weapon swing and movement are simple, the equipment you obtain over time are diverse and situationally useful. It’s a game that rewards adaptability; swapping to the appropriate equipment according to the environment and enemies you encounter will make fights easier. Whether wading through water or killing fast monsters, there is probably an item that will make obstacles easier to surmount.
  As you get further in the game, overpowered combinations of equipment become available and I love it. After cautiously navigating every encounter up to that point, there was an incredible relief in simply rolling over every enemy that once gave me grief.

  The need to frequently swap equipment, however, also means you have to navigate the inventory often. It’s cumbersome.
  You have to press ‘down’ and ‘up’ to trudge through your extensive lists of items. Even though these are partitioned in helpful categories, these categories are each a single, long vertical column. Most of the items you’ll frequently equip or consume are in 4 categories: weapons, spells, items, and equipment.
  You cannot skip ahead by jumping several items at a time. You cannot use your mouse. The only QoL in inventory navigation is the ability to change the sorting order and marking items as “favourites”. Though it’s better than nothing, the “favourites” feature simply keeps your items at the top of each long list, and still requires many button presses since you’ll likely want to keep several “favourites” (maybe six per category). Furthermore, when you want to try new items, it’ll take a while to find.
  It’s a small frustration that grates on you as you keep playing on.
  Fortunately, the game took me about 10 hrs to beat — including all side objectives, some frivolous achievements, and grinding for equipment and healing items.

[h2]Metroidvania, but is it Hard?[/h2]
  Expanding on gameplay a little more, there’s the matter of difficulty. Having beat the game on “Recommended”, I would say I had a comfortably tense experience.

  You can pause to heal in the middle of battle, but these are two key limitations that hinder such boring brute force. Firstly, the most common healing items regenerate 1 HP per second. Secondly, instant heals are expensive and tedious to obtain in large quantities. Not impossible, but tedious.

  On the first encounter with a new enemy, you are given room to fight it on its own, allowing you to learn its behaviour and abilities. You are then continually introduced to new combinations of enemies, each addition a compounding threat to your life. Fast enemies allow slow ones to attack. Some hinder your movements. Nearly every enemy can kill you if you carelessly swing at them. 

  If you die, you lose your progress up to your last save point. In a strangely refreshing way, this classic way of handling death works well. Given the increasing prevalence of ‘running to your corpse to take back your money’ in newer games, I think I like restarting with all your money and items still on you. The consumables you spent before death will return, so you don’t have to worry about making subsequent retries unnecessarily difficult. Put in combination with the autosave point right before boss fights, I never felt unduly punished for messing up.

  There is a hardcore mode, and new challenge modes unlock after beating the game, but I have not played them, so I cannot comment on those.

[h2]Is it Good?[/h2]
  All in all, it’s rather [u]difficult to recommend[/u]. Lost Ruins’ most interesting feature as a metroidvania is that it rewards the player’s adaptability just as much as their skill with the controls. Yet, this very selling point is hindered by tedious menu navigation as you frequently swap out your equipment.
  Its difficulty is well paced. Its visuals are as you see on the store page.
  It’s not a must-buy, but you might like this.

A fun little Metroidvania with only a handful of very minor stumbling blocks.

As the biggest pro, the spire artwork and animation is consistently amazing. Light sources reflect dynamically on the characters which gives the scenes an incredible feeling of depth. Attack animations have a good amount of heft to them, though slower two-handed animations look a bit floaty instead of giving a feeling of 'gravity' to the swing arc. For enemies, all attacks are well telegraphed and simple to read.

Combat has an odd mix of slightly floaty weapons with punishingly strict committal, though enemies are forced just as much to watch their attack whiff as you jab them in the back with a dagger, which makes the combat 'fair' for both parties, at least as long as you manage to keep it to a 1v1. Fighting multiple enemies at once is more often than not suicidal and sometimes you best choice is to run away or leave and reenter the room, resetting all still living enemies while dead ones remain temporarily disposed of (moving through enough rooms will revive all enemies in passed rooms). Weapons can feel somewhat floaty because one-handed and two-handed weapons are swung in an arc, but that arc has a steady speed throughout the entire animation, which can make especially slow attack swings feel very weak and weightless. Since being able to modify the swing speed through equipment is an option, I'm not sure if there is an elegant solution to that however.

I think the biggest roadblock a lot of people will face getting used to combat isn't its grounded attacks, but the fact that attacking mid-jump will completely void all horizontal momentum, meaning that if you attack while jumping forward you will just drop straight down instead. This paired with how the game likes to place ranged enemies across precarious jumps makes platforming a lot more dangerous than one would expect from a very platforming-focused metroidvania.

The typical solution to that of course represent magic and the disposable single-use wands that litter the environment. Magic is tied to MP which does not naturally regenerate, meaning you have to rely on consumables to refresh your MP or use equipment with provides you with some level of MP recovery. Wands are a reasonably abundant resource, but they are still limited in use, so they're best reserved for situations where melee would be too dangerous to commit to or open a handful of doors that require magic to activate their respective levers.

For the minor stumbling blocks I brought up in the beginning, while combat is pretty fun once you get the hang of it, the game has somewhat of an over-reliance on status effects and DoTs. Pretty much any attack won't just deal flat damage, but also give you increasingly long stacks of bleed, burn or poison, freeze you in place, invert your controls, and so forth. On Veteran difficulty these can also stack repeatedly on additional hits, frequently providing you with DoT effects that exceed even your maximum possible HP. Most ofthese effects can be countered and even temporarily negated with consumables, but in the heat of combat it can feel rather frustrating to have defeated a a single enemy but losing several items just to counter the DoT and replenish the health you've lost just as the result of burning.

Traps and trickery are our best allies in this game, learning which enemies are too dangerous to take head-on and how to bypass and/or defeat them without even allowing them to fight back are typically your best choices.

TL;DR: 6/10. A reasonably challenging and fun Metroidvania that has good replay value thanks to additional difficulties and game modes. It's short and sweet. Definitely worth a try.

I'll start with the critiques first:
- Air combat sucks. You will drop straight down if you try to attack midair, making it largely unusable. 
- Magic dominates. Magic quickly scales above the other fight methods and becomes absolutely broken. [spoiler] Especially on bosses[/spoiler].
- No I-Frames. You will take hits, and immediately get juggled with additional hits. Worse on higher difficulty.

Now to some positives:
- The game has charming visuals and a good soundtrack.
- So much cute stuff to go around, I almost feel guilty having to kill them.
- Dodging and blocking are very reliable, and most of the time you can tell which will work and where.
- The different game modes are exciting and encourages repeat playthroughs. [spoiler] Especially Boss Mode [/spoiler].
- Set items that allows you to experiment with different builds.
- The game is challenging, but more often than not fair to the player.
- Multiple endings. While not major, still a nice touch and satisfying.

Perhaps what the game lacks is the ability to chat with NPCs who inhabit the world. Shopkeepers will not say anything to you once their scripted dialogue is over and only offer services. It felt like a missed opportunity to flesh them out along with the world.

The gallery you unlock is on the smaller side and you quickly unlock it all. I would have liked to see more artwork of the different designs for the enemies and locations. As it is now, it's underwhelming. Made worse by the fact that a few artworks are just rearrangements of each other, which feels pretty lazy.

Some plot beats seem to go unfinished, which makes me wonder if the game was rushed of the writers just didn't care. [spoiler] You meet a ghost who tells you to pass on a message to the first boss, as they knew each other. Once you encounter the boss, the protagonist just completely blanks on said message and the fight goes on without this being resolved. [/spoiler] It just feels like a dead end and is disappointing.

Similarly, the game lies to you in one area that I don't know if it's a glitch, oversight, or intended design. [spoiler] When the holy knight tells you that you are allowed to open the golden chests, she will still attack you if you do. And the dialogue before the fight is the same as if you opened the chest before she gave you her permission. [/spoiler] So that's weird.

Boss Mode feels quite a bit shorter than the main modes. [spoiler] You are given quite a few tools to blitz through the game quicker. But it feels like an afterthought since it plays mostly the same but with altered dialogues. Most NPCs are completely removed from the world for no apparent reason. All the bosses are identical which is not very clever. [/spoiler] It's still fun and an absolute cherry on top to the existing story.

However, none of this kills the enjoyment for me. I've already binged the game to satisfaction and I see myself picking this up again to try and beat the other game modes I've not tried yet. I recommend this to anyone who likes the Metroidvania genre.

This is a hard game to recommend. I don't usually review games I haven't beat it, neither for games I refunded, however, if the first few hours of the game doesn't hook you in, it's a bit hard to continue playing...

This is specially the case with Lost Ruins. A game that visually looks incredible, reminding me of the Momodora series by Bombservice. Despite the great looking visuals, the biggest problem of this game is the pace. I'm talking about "constant open inventory" kind of games.

In this game, there are a lot of things you have to be aware of, environmental things that can damage you, healing items that heal or cure effects, and so on. You can also use different weapons that vary your attack speed and things like that. Some enemies work better with certain weapons, while others are best approached with complete different playstyles.

The game does not have any sort of preset switcher or ways to quickly switch things, as pointed out in other reviews that have beat the game. I stopped playing the game after my first hour or so, those hours were mostly going into the inventory screen to change gear and stuff, not much about actually playing the game. Every time that I had to do something on the inventory screen made the game feel incredibly slow.

Some of the items I unlocked seems like they could simply be passive items instead of items you have to equip to have that effect applied to you. One of those items can be easily exploited, being a Ring that reduces your Max Health, but regens your health upon wearing it. I think there's also another negative upon wearing it that I forgot what it does now.

Lost your health? Well, you can go to the inventory screen once again, equip that Ring, return to the game, wait for the health regen, go back to the inventory yet again, equip an item with a better bonus (since you won't be needing the Ring while at full health), advance a little to the room before you get damaged to something that you would prefer to get damaged instead of relying with constant inventory opening for every little thing in this game (as there's many different environmental damage types toward your adventure). Repeat the process.

Even if you don't constant switch to this Ring (either play without it or play with it equipped at all times), you will still need to be constantly using your inventory screen to use specific spells to deal with specific things blocking your path, to defeat enemies easier, to heal yourself, and so on. No matter your playstyle, you will have to rely heavily on the inventory screen in this game, and with no way to quickly switch things, and no preset-loadouts, it's really hard to get the pace of this game flowing. The great visuals stop being your focus, and the letters of your inventory screen ends up being what's shown on screen most of the time, sadly.

Your attack speed, depending on the weapon you equip, is also pretty slow. Your character goes into a complete halt when attacking. I wouldn't mind this very much if it wasn't for the constant menu-ing in this game. I really want to like this game, I really do, specially because of those great looking visuals, but it's really hard to continue playing after you realize what you'll be doing in the entire game:

Opening the inventory screen every few seconds or so.

The enemies are also unforgiving, as they can quickly drain your health due to the lack (or very little) invincibility frames. Combine this with things I have previously mentioned, you want to rely the maximum with your current arsenal, and the things you have obtained. Healing yourself with the Ring is a huge bonus and it's hard to overlook when so many things in this game can damage you in either fair or unfair ways.

So yeah, this is one of those reviews that the writer wants to like the game, but just can't. I really really want to like this game, but, it doesn't feel like I'm playing a game when I'm constantly switching my arsenal instead of doing anything on it.

There are also a few other nitpicks I want to bring up:

- There's no way to disable voices in the game. These are tied to Sound Effects volume slider (you can disable Music and Sound Effects separately). This game doesn't have voice acting for dialogue, but your character will shout things when doing certain things like getting hit, being killed, blocking, etc., and it can get annoying after a while. I wish I didn't had to turn off all sounds to get rid of the voices / grunts that my character does when doing action X, Y, Z.

- You can equip a shield that, upon successfully blocking, the character uses the same voice line when you take damage. This feels pretty weird, to be honest. It should either have a different voice clip or no voice at all. Just a loud "blocking" noise would be sufficient in this case.

Incredibly player-hostile design, and not in a hard-but fair Hollow Knight way. The game features slow, clunky movement  affected by barely visible surface effects (like slimy, oily, or simply wet floors), and a useless dodge roll with a painfully long recovery that leaves you wide open. The combat is built for maximum frustration, with even the “fastest” weapons being painfully slow. Anything that deals any kind of damage takes a comically long time to deliver a blow, while enemies have no trouble spamming projectiles and lightning-quick attacks.
Aside from some charming and well-animated sprites, the visuals are murky and hard to discern, so you often aren't even sure what hurt you. The game doesn't give you any way to heal or replenish MP early on, leaving you to scavenge a menagerie of borderline useless items that heal you a couple of HP at a time.

And then there are abnormal status effects. Every, and I mean EVERY enemy gives you abnormal status with their attacks. Got hit by an insect - poison! Got hit by a goblin - bleed! Stepped into a barely visible puddle of water - wet (enjoy that 50% movement speed reduction for the next 5 seconds in a middle of a fight). All effects are unavoidable and instant, and all of them will absolutely kill you in seconds if you don't pause the game, open inventory, scroll to items tab, scroll down through a long list of confusing junk, and find the exact thing that heals this particular status effect. Close menu and get a new status effect right away.

Despite how frustratingly difficult and un-rewarding the “normal” mode is, the game doesn't even deem it pertinent to give you an ending, as, you see – you only get endings if you play on “veteran” or higher. 

On top of it all, the game is confusingly horny, to the point where I feel like it was originally meant to be an H-game that got neutered for wider release.

Survival Tips for those looking to pick up this game

 - Speed is always better than power, because stun locks make everything one-sided. This also applies to you. 
 - The healing amulet is your friend
 - The shield is your good friend
 - The roll is your best friend.
- Healing amulet + Belt is the game's internal easy mode as it means you can't die unless you're really bad at dodging. 
 - Combat for stronger enemies is the really boring process of roll-attack-repeat. This is probably what's causing people's complaints for this game. It's slow. Especially when it comes to area hazards where you have to burn them away, and then wait for the fire to die down. There are trinkets to counter this, but, until you get them, its a lot of waiting. 
- I managed to beat the game fairly quickly once I switched my build to shield + dagger. The shield is great and even works on bosses in ways that make them stupid easy. The dagger's speed lets you get in hits without getting countered, but the range means you'll have to space and time your rolls so you're close enough for a hit. 
- If you want to use magic, you can...but only if you like constantly going into menus to restore your MP or swap to another consumable wand. Magic Sucks. Get the Knife.

Overall, the game is okay, but I wouldn't call it great or even very good. Its short, its simple, its awkward, and its the kind of game where you're constantly looking for the quick kill on otherwise mundane enemies and bosses.

This game has a lot going for it, particularly the visuals.  The lighting effects and animations are particularly impressive.  But the gameplay has some very significant issues that I have a hard time getting past.  The combat is slow, and ponderous, and at first this seemed like a good design choice and I was enjoying the different pace.  But as I played more, and got through a few bosses, I started seeing that the combat was actually problematic.  It feels like you're fighting in quicksand, with every action taking far loo many frames to complete.  When you combine that with the fact that every hit staggers you, and that there are actually ZERO iframes in the game, you find yourself facing frustrating death after frustrating death at the hands of a single hit that started a chain reaction of further hits that you have no ability to avoid.  It feels like a juggle-heavy fighting game, where getting hit with a single punch can lead into a 20 second long air juggle that ultimately takes 90% of your health before you get to control your character again.

There is magic in the game, and the spells are very powerful, but you don't recover health or mana when you hit a save point or safe room (like SotN or most other Metroidvanias), so you don't get to cast but 2 or 3 spells and then you have to wait until you find another mana potion or something to enable another spell or two.  It's too bad, because incorporating spells would make the combat less of a trudge.  

The same thing goes for items.  There are throwing items like knives and bottles, but they are extremely finite.  It's not based on an energy system or anything replenishable like most Metroidvanias, they are literally - you find 3 knives.  You can throw three times and then they are gone forever.  You also only get two items you can equip at a time, which includes your melee weapon and shield if you want one.  So, you can choose to have a sword and shield equipped, but that is it.  No throwing knives, bottles, arrows, etc.  If you want to use one of those limited number items, you have to forego a shield, which is insanity since everything in the game can easily kill you.  

All in all, there are some good things in here but ultimately the combat killed it for me.

I should start by saying that I really don't want to write a negative review of this game, because parts of it are very good. The Art, which everyone has already touched on is one of the best uses of particle effects and lighting that I've seen in a 2D game, and the level design is, for what it is, actually very good. I did enjoy myself when exploring, both while going through the first time, and when going back for all the chests that I skipped (There's a reason to do so, it's explained in game). 

Unfortunately, I can't say the same about the combat, and for a game that is so heavily based around it, it's a deal breaker. To put it simply, it feels as though the players move-set and the enemies where designed for different games. The player has a simple move-set, with slow weapon swings even on fast weapons and a dodge that has I-frames but also a very long recovery, which indicate that the game is one based primarily around spacing and avoiding enemies with similarly long windups and cool-downs. 

Many of the enemies however didn't seem to get the memo, and attack so fast that in the time it takes for some of the player's slower weapons to swing, they can finish the recovery on their last attack, start up a new one, and finish it before the player can hit them. This more or less results in a combat system that encourages not skill, but finding the cheesiest possible strategy and then spamming it regardless of how boring it is to play, and make no mistake, standing out of range of enemies, hiding behind a shield while the enemies get killed by spinning swords isn't fun.

Perhaps this kind of clunky combat would work if the game was based primarily around avoiding enemies, and indeed many horror games achieve success in this way quite well, but this game is a different beast, as it has fairly involved 2 or 3 stage boss fights, in which the sub-par combat is left to fend for itself, devoid of any good level design to hide behind.

To compound this, the game has a fairly significant number of smaller design issues that make it quite frequently a chore to play. On that front, the rest of this review is just going to be list of my more minor issues and some of my ideas on how they might be resolved.
[list]
[*]Due to the way healing items are distributed, I sometimes found myself farming healing items, since I had no where near enough money to buy them. Just add an Estus flask, or failing that, at least make healing item drops more consistent in late game areas. I know it's a bit of a cop-out to just steal a mechanic, especially one from Dark Souls but From's been using it since Dark Souls 1 for a reason.
[*]A fairly early game item allows the player to get a full heal more or less when ever they want so long as they have access to a portal ([spoiler] I'm talking about the purifier [/spoiler]), but requires just standing there for upwards of 40 seconds in the later parts of the game. A mid game item that gave the player a full heal when a portal is interacted with would quite handily resolve the issue.
[*]The game's combat often requires the player to switch equipment and weapons in order to deal with changing circumstances, as many enemies are markedly easier to fight with certain weapons/spells/passives. Loadout hot-switching would be very useful, or failing that, at least the ability to favorite items in the menu such that they always sort to the top
[*]Checkpoints only save the first time you pass them unless you fully unload the area. While I understand why someone would want to avoid a save in certain circumstances, not being able to re-save at all is very unhelpful when for example, fighting a boss and wanting to go in with a specific loadout that makes the boss more manageable. An easy solution here would be making it so one could reactivate checkpoints manually after they've been activated.
[/list]

Definitely my least favorite part of the game, and it's basically all there is to the game. To call this game "challenging" is inaccurate. It's intentionally designed to frustrate you.

- Attack animations take forever to execute and recover from, while enemies attack with lightning speed and have massive windows for hitting you. 
- You don't get i-frames if you're hit, so some enemies can one shot you, by actually hitting you 5+ times in rapid succession. All you have to do is get hit that first time. 
- HP and MP don't regenerate unless you use items. There's no camp to restore HP and MP. You'll be able to cast a spell twice, and then have to spend money on items to cast again.

- - 2. Actually play the game, and just die. And then sit through all the cutscenes again.
