Lost Ruins is not a bad game, but it struggles with conflicting design choices that prevent it from being a great experience.

The game begins as a challenging, horror-inspired experience. Traps can kill you in two hits, healing items are scarce, and monsters are tough unless you manage a sneak attack. This tense, survival-horror atmosphere holds until around the second boss. At that point, the game shifts dramatically, offering an abundance of powerful tools and weapons, transitioning into a more action-oriented style.

Both styles—horror and action—can be enjoyable on their own. However, the abrupt transition between them weakens the overall experience. By the third boss, the challenge diminishes significantly. The final bosses can be beaten by simply turning invisible and attacking a few times, stripping away any remaining sense of difficulty and horror.

This shift is unfortunate because the game's early survival-horror design shows real promise, similar to what games like Fear and Hunger achieve. However, the developers' desire to give players as many tools as possible undermines the initial tension and challenge.

On the positive side, the animation style is very well done, with clever little details in every character's movement. Whether or not this style appeals to you is subjective, but the trailer gives a clear idea of what to expect. The small amount of story is enjoyable, and the characters have just enough personality to be engaging during their brief appearances. While not groundbreaking, it feels like genuine effort was put into the narrative and characters.

On the downside, some of the music was genuinely headache-inducing, and my controller would randomly vibrate for no apparent reason after starting the game, which was frustrating.

Overall, Lost Ruins feels like someone's first serious attempt at creating a complex video game—a project they likely learned a lot from. Thankfully, the game's short length (about eight hours) means its bigger issues don't completely overshadow the fun.

If you like the visual style and aren't too concerned about having a true survival-horror experience, there's still plenty to enjoy in Lost Ruins.

- There are so many vendors and items to buy but almost nothing drops gold???

- Why would you use two different save methods to act as your checkpoints??? The computers let you hard save and the many green statues act as auto-save checkpoints but cannot be triggered a second time? So if you auto-save before a boss get ready to have to re-configure all your gear if you die every single time.

- Speaking of green statues why don't they refill your HP/MP? I get the whole "survival" aspect but when gold is non-existent having to buy any kind of consumables is a chore and a half.

- The dodge roll is atleast 50 recovery frames too long, some enemies just straight up attack faster than you can after dodging their initial attack so rolling seems kind of pointless other than abusing I-frames.

- Because there is no XP/leveling system actually fighting and killings mobs is made kind of pointless other than to watch the nice sprites do cool things.

Hopefully the devs can update the game to fix these glaring issues but until then its a fat NO from me which is a real shame because I was looking forward to this game based on the art alone but that's all it has going for it at the moment. I'd be more than happy to help in any way I can to address some of these issues with the devs but if you're in the market for an incredibly solid Metroidvania experience check out Unworthy or Blasphemous, those two games are way more polished and Unworthy was a one man job.

Edit: To clarify because a lot of the comments have pointed to this particular point as a way to discredit the review, I'm not saying that the game absolutely NEEDS a leveling system. What I'm pointing out is that there is no reward for killing enemies apart from some drops. 

Towards the end of the game, I found that it was a lot more worthwhile to spam the invisibility spell with mana regen equipment to just bypass enemies. Because of how clunky the combat is, especially if you're playing on the harder difficulties you waste more resources fighting than just bypassing which isn't particularly good game design. I want to have a reason to kill enemies beyond getting another arrow bundle for a bow I won't ever use.

Clearly some people have very strong opinions about this review and are very vocal in the comments, we can agree to disagree on the state of this game but for the 20 ish dollar price tag I feel there are currently better options on the market and the game being tagged with the "Metroidvania" tag might be misleading to some and I hope this review can give them a clear picture about MY experience with the game compared to the many other Metroidvania games I've played.

Oh boy is this game a mixed bag! Let’s start with the first thing though: this game is NOT a metroidvania in any stretch of the imagination. It’s a pretty straightforward action-adventure game. 

Now that said let’s just skip to some of the problems and even dealbreakers with this game. 

Problems. 

1. The combat is stiff and very clunky. Now you may like this so it really depends but I would have liked it to be much more fluid and smooth. For me it took some time and many deaths before a learned it and in the end I can somewhat appreciate it. 

2. There’s save points and check points. Now at a save point you can obviously save your progress (logic) and the check points are there to restart you when you die. But here’s the problem. You can only activate a check point once and if you choose to go back and save and then pass the check point again it won’t activate! You now restart from your save point. Now to  the real issue, let’s say you activate a check point and then you fight a boss. You may have a different setup for some bosses (different weapons, different magic you get what I mean) so you change your setup before that boss fight. And now you die and you go back to retry (from the check point) and you notice the all the changes you have made is reseted to what you had before so you have to do the same changes EVERY TIME after you die. The only way to save the changes is at a save point. This is infuriating to say the least. 

3. The achievements are totally broken! I mean they straight up doesn’t work! If this is important to you move this to the “deal breaker” section. 

The deal breaker! 

Now this last one is an absolutely deal breaker for me. You see I started playing this game on my Steam Deck and I was planning on finishing the game on my PC once I got back home. But no such luck, the cloud saves doesn’t work. And I’ve tried everything under the sun the game refuses to sync up to my PC. This is the one thing that tipped me over for: “it’s a ok adventure game I can recommend to some people” to “nope! That’s one more technical issue I won’t accept”! 

So if any of my complaints is a deal breaker to you just stay away from this game or at least wait to a sale and/or an update…..maybe it’ll be good game in a couple of months who knows?

A short metriodvania that delivers on what it sells: a hard side-scrolling dungeon-crawler with cute(ish) monster girls of varying attitudes. It's okay, I am not a fan of the mix of artwork and not a pure focus on sprite-artwork.

[h1] Things to Expect [/h1]

[list]
    [*] A semi-predictable story.
    [*] Punishing combat that gradually becomes easier.
    [*] Very good sprite-work in lighting, effects, and enviroment.
    [*] Extra modes and multiple endings.
    [*] You can sell things to merchants, including the vending machines.
[/list]

[h1] Aesthetics [/h1]
While not the best sprite-work I have seen, it is certainly of high quality! It has the Shantae-issue of hip-shaking and nearly everything dressed in a school-girl's uniform. The music is there and it works to help the mood of each area in the game.

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]
This game is hard, and this difficulty comes from enemy damage along with a limited kit at the start of the game. As you explore and overcome, you gain various means to make combat easier along with managing damage and magic point scores.

Unfortunately, this is where the Metriodvania qualities end as you gain no extra movement tools, and optional paths to loot either take dynamite(or a fireball spell), or a weapon/spell with long reach (Chain Lightning). Traveling the world is made very simple with a teleport system. The real challenges come from boss fights, but depending on your kit can also be made trivial.

[h1] Story and Characters [/h1]
There is a very simple story here, with creepy implications later on. However, it loses marks from the extra artwork and dialogues you have with various monster girls through-out the game. There is plenty of environmental story-telling just from the sprite-work, but that is lost the farther along you get in the game. The dialogue takes away from the story by explaining the story, which ruins any interest in trying to figure things out yourself. I would have liked it a lot more if the story was told via exploring and looking around, rather than some anime cut-scene girl being glib and just explaining things.

[h1] Opinion and Conclusions [/h1]
I like Metriodvanias, and a good challenge. I disliked the conversation artwork, and the lean on cheesecake character design. Tits have a habit of tarnishing something that was otherwise pretty good. Not to say that this is a bad game, nor a game to be taken super seriously, but it sadly does not marry its over-the-top presentation with its design completely.

Oof, this is rough.

The game has really pretty pixel art, visually Lost Ruins is great, but on the gameplay side it's just not fun.
Your attacks are slow and even the largest weapons barely have enough reach to hit an enemy before they are able to get our their *much* faster attacks.

Also almost every enemy in this game will apply some sort of debuff onto you, like bleed or poison damage, which can last up to 30 seconds for certain enemies, dealing 1 damage per second, when that's more than your total HP.
But hey, there's a ton of consumables that let you heal a tiny bit and remove such status effects.
That however means you constantly have to go in and out of your inventory, looking for the right consumable to get rid of effects every time you get hit by an enemy.
And again, enemies get much quicker attack animations than you, so the chance of getting hit isn't exactly low.

And what do you get for defeating enemies?
Well since there's no XP system or anything like that, if you're lucky they may drop another consumable...
Sometimes, but only rarely will enemies drop some coins you can use to buy equipment at vendors.
But prices are super high and the amount of gold dropped by enemies is tiny.
Like a piece of equipment may cost you like 150G, but every 5 or so enemies you may get 5 gold to drop.

To keep it short, gameplay isn't fun at all.

Sadly, the story and characters are just as bad.
It's already weird enough to see all these girls running around in japanese schoolgirl outfits in a dark fantasy setting, but the story revolving around summoning girls from another world for some sacrifice is just extremely threadbare.
The main character, merely named "Heroine" is as milquetoast as they get.
She never has a single interesting thing to say in dialogue nor does she react to things like characters getting straight up killed in front of her.
There's a small handful of other characters here, mainly they're the bosses, but their writing is just as terrible.

It's such a shame, since the they really seemed to have put a lot of work in the pixel art for Lost Ruins, but everything beside the visuals, this is terrible.

Wouldn't recommend this at all sadly.

[i]Low Tier, Rides the Edge of Recommending[/i]

5/10. Probably best described as a 2D adventure game. This is not your typical skilled action combat centric metroidvania. Not worth your time unless you have nothing left to play. 

Instead of going into every issue I have with Lost Ruins I'll summarize it overall. The game isn't broken but it puts forth the minimum effort to make just about every aspect barely passable. This genre is too competitive for these kind of entrants to be positive recommendations.

While the game is fun in some cases.  The storyline is a bit meh, and the exploration tends to actually be held back by the game mechanics itself.  There appears to be some basic concepts that I thought was a bit out of place for a dungeon/exploration/platforming game.

I do think that the direct "drop" of the character while in mid air attacking plays in a cheap way to increase the difficulty.  The character should dedicate herself to the jump and while I think the jumps are sufficient, the attacks to bring a 90deg drop and wallstop mid air is an artificial cheap way of making this game harder.

I also find another artificial difficulty in this game where there's very little money to buy items to assist.  This tends to create this "hoarding" type mentality and I don't actually use items or tools to help when it's too consumable.  I'll farm for items like chicken, and the difficult part is that I gotta teleport to respawn items.  This tends to get in the way of progress and also delays what is suppose to be just straight exploration.

There are just straight forward game design flaws in this game, and at full price I would have never bought this game.  I do love the art style and I do love the characters, but the artificial difficulty bumps that are just due to bad and lazy level design is quite "annoying" to play through.  I will complete this game, but so far after maybe 5 hours of it -- it's a little uninspiring with the game mechanics. 

boss battles are fun at least, but the artificial handicaps get in the way.  The only saving grace is that respawns are close items are recovered when death occurs (eg it just reloads your auto save).
Controller configuration gets annoying, I don't understand why the button configs on the controller changes the movement of the tabs?  This is a good example of lazy programming and not putting an extra routine in to properly map buttons to separate the way buttons map between menu and actual game play.

(eg. I don't like spells on left or right buttons, so I move it to right button and right trigger, but now the TABS on the menu are mapped to left button and left trigger -- this is plain lazy for a game developer)

I hope this gets properly patched and the devs look into making some of the gameplay mechanics better so that we don't get stalled by bad fetch quests and bad mechanics that artificially make the game longer and harder. 

One other item that bothers me is the lack of MP heal drops.  enemies tend to drop more health than mana recovery drops.  I tend to not even use spells if MP is used up since there's no way to heal and with the lack of resources (being unable to properly buy items without farming for hours) there's no reason for me to stick around and do anything or even look at vending machines.  MP heal drops should be a bit more often if you want players to use spells, also larger mp pool would be nicer considering you have spells that cost 12MP given a 20pt pool.  this is not even good if you don't allow for HP/MP recovery at autosave spots (which is also another artificial difficulty bump). 

Better planning and more enemy placements in a room would be nice - large empty room with 1-2 mobs with platforming is too little.  Even with no XP gains, it would be nice to just be able to do more.  Makes the inclusive fetch quests a bit more entertaining.  Also RESPAWNS, I gotta warp out and back to do a respawn, this is just meh.

I'm reluctant to admit that I enjoyed this game since it was obviously made for weeboos, what with you playing as a short skirted schoolgirl that can find a swimsuit as an alternate costume, fighting other girls as big titted bosses (some of which are completely naked) in pretty generic dungeons with generic dark fantasy enemies. Not to mention, the generic amnesiac main protagonist seems to lack a moral compass as they go around slaughtering enemies while acting all kiddy and innocent. Ultimately, the game really doesn't even have an interesting story so I definitely think catering to weeboos was a central draw to it's presentation.

Mechanically, the game shines with pretty solid effects and animations. The base combat consisting of your girl swinging swords in an arc of various timings based on the kinds of weapons you use adds some strategy to combat by forcing you to get the timings right, which can be a lot of fun, and there's neat gimmicks like pretty well done fire physics, all apparently done in the Unity engine. I'm not a big fan of all the status effects you can incur from so many enemies' attacks, and it's got that "Symphony of the Night" problem where it's not long before you find a sword that's guaranteed to be your preference over others, trivialising other loot you find which is the game's only real progress draw, what with the lack of a levelling system (which I also like). Being a Metroidvania game, I also inevitably came to points where I got lost, which is where I'm at now in the game. Lacking a real interesting story or characters that aren't terribly written under-aged waifus, I can't say I'm that motivated to move forward either. 

The smooth animations and pixel graphics do look pretty good, but the game might've been optimised terribly, as it bricked the computer played it on before I got the one I'm typing on now. 

6/10 - I would play it again, and even recommend it to some, but there's likely better Metroidvanias that don't rely on schoolgirls as their draw, so thumbs down.

I would've liked this game more if it doesn't turn into "opening inventory simulator". This game offers you the versatility to use anything towards your enemies, whether they're swords, magic attacks, or environment interactions like setting up oil on fire or freezing enemies inside water. 

The problem with this is, there is no presets for you to make to quickly switch from one to another; you have to open your inventory to switch to the weapon or magic you want to use in that situation, and then switch back to whatever you're using before because it's a playstyle you're comfortable with. Perhaps you see water on the floor and you don't want to be electrocuted or be frozen, so you open your inventory to equip the swimsuit. Or perhaps you encounter enemies that does bleed damage, so you open inventory to consume bleed removal foods or wear armor that negates bleed debuff. Or perhaps you're just low on HP, you open your inventory to consume foods.

All of this makes the pacing very slow, on top of the combat being slow already in the first place. I don't mind if I have to commit to the slow sword swinging animations, but what I don't like is having to constantly pause the game to switch stuff around. Sure, I can just stick to one type of build all the time, but in a game where the game can be very punishing because of the character's low HP, no i-frames upon getting hit, and HP and MP are not replenished unless you consume foods, it's better to try and take advantage of the situation you're in.

After all, this game has a popup at the beginning of the run that says the game wants the player to think to solve problems they encounter. I want to do that, but the constant pausing to switch stuff around due to lack of preset options is ruining the experience. The unfortunate part about this game is, there is a bonus mode that fixes this problem, but you have to beat the game first.
